demand.angle: What Mac users — especially developers — actually request and complain about regarding disk space and cleaning, with concrete features, frustrations, "freed N GB" stories, willingness-to-pay, and trust signals.
demand.summary: Mac users split into two cleaning camps with sharply different needs. (1) General users panic over an opaque "System Data" bucket (often 50-150 GB) they don't understand and are afraid to touch — they mostly want a trustworthy explainer + safe one-click reclaim, and they're deeply skeptical of CleanMyMac, which the technical crowd labels scareware/bloat that "duplicates what macOS already does" for ~$35-40/yr. (2) Developers have a concrete, well-understood problem: dev toolchains silently hoard 50-150 GB in known paths (Xcode DerivedData, iOS DeviceSupport, CoreSimulator, node_modules, Gradle/Android, Docker, Cargo, Homebrew caches). They know exactly what to delete and that it's regenerable — they just want a fast, transparent tool that finds it across all projects, shows sizes, marks safe-vs-risky, and never touches source code. The dominant frustrations are: subscriptions (huge — people loudly prefer one-time/open-source), fear of breaking things, bloat/scareware marketing, and tools that "barely move the needle" on the hidden dev caches. Willingness-to-pay is real but capped: one-time $9.99-29 is celebrated; recurring $35-40/yr is resented. Trust signals that win: open source, "show exactly what will be deleted" preview, no account required, notarized, local-only, small footprint, and safe/danger tiering.

findings.point: Developers' #1 disk hog is Xcode: DerivedData, iOS DeviceSupport, CoreSimulator, and Archives routinely total 30-150+ GB in known, safe-to-delete paths
findings.detail: Concrete path/size table that recurs across sources: ~/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData (10-50 GB, safe, auto-rebuilds), ~/Library/Developer/CoreSimulator/Devices (20-150 GB; the folder 'can easily reach 20-30 GB or more'), ~/Library/Developer/Xcode/iOS DeviceSupport (10-40 GB; each iOS version dir is 2-5 GB and 10+ accumulate over 2-3 yrs), ~/Library/Developer/Xcode/Archives (5-30 GB), ~/Library/Caches/CocoaPods and ~/Library/Caches/org.swift.swiftpm (1-5 GB each). Canonical commands users run: rm -rf ~/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData/* and xcrun simctl delete unavailable. iOS devs report 50-100 GB consumed after a year of development. This is the single most actionable feature target: a one-click 'Xcode reclaim' that knows these exact paths and which are safe.

findings.point: Concrete 'I freed N GB by deleting X' stories — devs reclaim 80-200+ GB and know exactly what worked
findings.detail: 168 GB freed (257→88 GB) by deleting ~/Library/Android/sdk/system-images, ~/.gradle/caches, Xcode DerivedData, iOS DeviceSupport, and old simulators (xcrun simctl delete unavailable). 80 GB freed with DevCleaner broken down as: Xcode DerivedData 35 GB, Android Studio/Gradle 22 GB, Flutter builds 12 GB, IDE caches 8 GB, logs/junk 3 GB (Mac had only 10 GB free, was sluggish). npkill (npx npkill, deletes node_modules interactively) testimonials: 'one user saved over 200GB', another 'deleted 50 GB+ so far'. node_modules is typically 200 MB-1 GB per project and accumulates to 15+ GB across abandoned repos. The recurring narrative: a dev hits near-zero free space, scans, and is shocked how much was hidden in caches they forgot existed.

findings.point: The biggest emotional frustration for general users: a huge, opaque 'System Data' bucket they're afraid to touch
findings.detail: macOS lumps caches, logs, local Time Machine snapshots, iOS device backups, and temp files into 'System Data', which users see balloon to 100-200+ GB with no explanation. A healthy size is ~12-25 GB; >30 GB signals stale caches/snapshots, >100 GB demands cleanup. Top real culprits users discover: local Time Machine snapshots (tens of GB when backup drive disconnected), old iPhone/iPad backups (single backup 20-40 GB), stale app caches. Apple-forum threads show users with 'System data taking up 115GB' asking what is safe. The product opportunity: explain the bucket in plain language and surface the specific reclaimable sub-categories (snapshots, iOS backups, caches) with sizes — users want understanding before they'll click delete.

findings.point: Subscriptions are the single most-cited dealbreaker; one-time purchase and open-source are the loudest requests
findings.detail: CleanMyMac's ~$35-40/yr subscription drives explicit defection. A HN developer: 'built a $5.99 alternative to CleanMyMac because I was tired of paying $40/yr.' DevCleaner blog post explicitly contrasts itself with 'generic Mac cleaner apps that charge subscription fees' and the author trusted it because it's '100% Free and Open Source' with 'no hidden fees or subscriptions.' Pricing that the market celebrates: DaisyDisk $9.99 one-time ('worth every penny', 'no subscriptions or hidden fees', 'one of the easiest Mac utility recommendations'); DevCleaner Pro Lifetime $29 one-time (vs $9.99/yr); free tools (OmniDiskSweeper, GrandPerspective, AppCleaner, OnyX, npkill) are heavily recommended. CleanMyMac also generates auto-renewal/refund complaints (50+ on PissedConsumer over 3 yrs; unexpected $34.95 charges). Implication for spec: lead with one-time pricing; recurring will be punished in this category.

findings.point: Technical users distrust CleanMyMac-style cleaners as scareware/bloat that 'barely moves the needle' and may break things
findings.detail: HN themes: 'absolute JUNK', 'patronizing' marketing copy like 'awesomize your Mac', and 'software McCarthyism' (it flagged Russian-developer utilities as untrustworthy 'because they are russian'). Effectiveness complaint: one power user said it 'barely moved' their 220 GB of System Data because dev tools hide GBs in cache paths the app can't detect. Fear-of-breaking is real: Apple-forum users report 'had to reinstall macOS multiple times' and warn cache cleaners 'can interfere with critical system functions' / 'brick your Mac' by deleting needed components. Counter-evidence worth noting for the spec: CleanMyMac is in fact notarized and one detailed review found 'no complaints about it breaking Macs or deleting needed files' — so the fear is largely reputational/perception, which a trustworthy newcomer can win on by being transparent.

findings.point: Most-requested feature set for a developer-focused cleaner (synthesized from what tools advertise + what devs praise)
findings.detail: (1) Multi-toolchain scan across many projects at once — DevCleaner scans 23 toolchains incl. Xcode, Android/Gradle, Node/npm (~/.npm/_cacache), CocoaPods (~/Library/Caches/CocoaPods), Homebrew (~/Library/Caches/Homebrew), Flutter (~/.pub-cache), Go (~/Library/Caches/go-build), Rust (~/.cargo/registry/cache), Docker, plus AI tools (Ollama, LM Studio, Cursor, Claude, ChatGPT caches). (2) Size + last-used date per item with sort by size/recency. (3) Safe/Warning/Danger tiering so users know what regenerates vs what's risky (npkill marks apps like Spotify/Discord with a ⚠️ because deleting their node_modules breaks them). (4) Never touch source code — 'Source code is never targeted', 'only known cache and build artifact paths'. (5) One-click Quick Clean + optional auto-clean/smart triggers. (6) 'Project hibernation' / archive-and-restore idle projects (DevCleaner Pro). Treemap/sunburst visualization (DaisyDisk-style) is the most-praised UX for the 'where did my space go' job.

findings.point: Trust signals people explicitly look for before running a cleaner
findings.detail: Recurring trust requirements from the sources: open source / GitHub-visible code (cited as the reason the DevCleaner reviewer trusted it); 'show exactly what will be deleted' / preview before delete (CleanMyMac users specifically use the Review step; CodeCleaner offers 'free preview before deletion'); no account required (DevCleaner, CodeCleaner both advertise this); local-only processing, no cloud upload; Apple notarization; small footprint (DevCleaner is 4 MB); minimal/opt-out telemetry ('only bytes freed tracked; can be disabled'); and a restore/undo path (DevCleaner offers 'dry-run restore' for archived projects; regenerability messaging — 'Xcode will regenerate this automatically' — reduces fear). The absence of preview/undo and the presence of pushy upsell marketing are the fastest trust-killers.

findings.point: Hardware reality amplifies the pain: soldered, non-upgradeable, often small (256 GB) Apple Silicon SSDs
findings.detail: Developers repeatedly vent that modern Macs have soldered SSDs that can't be upgraded — 'I ran out of disk space on the (soldered in SSD) Mac. I can't delete anything.' Apple's pricing for storage upgrades pushes many devs onto 256/512 GB machines, so reclaiming 50-150 GB of dev caches isn't a nicety — it's what keeps the machine usable. Secondary modern irritants devs name: Apple Intelligence consuming ~5 GB 'despite telling it to fuck off', macOS 'leaking' ~20 GB into System Data, Mac App Store forcing installs into /Applications, and apps scattering files into 'arcane directories' beyond the .app bundle. This validates urgency/recurrence — it's not a one-time chore, it's a constant battle on capacity-constrained hardware.

findings.point: Competitive landscape and price anchors to position against
findings.detail: Free/loved: OmniDiskSweeper (simple largest-first list), GrandPerspective (free treemap, 'powerful but not friendly'), AppCleaner (uninstaller), OnyX (system maintenance), npkill/dustoff (CLI node_modules killers), Mole (MIT-licensed). Paid one-time (the sweet spot): DaisyDisk $9.99 (sunburst visualizer, scans disk in <30s, universally recommended), DevCleaner Pro $29 lifetime, CodeCleaner (free scan, paid cleanup). Subscription (resented): CleanMyMac ~$35-40/yr, Setapp bundle. Emerging dev/cache-focused entrants to watch: Clutterfall (Clean vs DeepClean modes for browser/chat/dev/AI caches), Devpurge, Cluttered. Gap to exploit: a transparent, one-time-priced, open-or-auditable tool that does both the general 'System Data explainer' job AND the deep developer-cache job in one app — most tools do only one half well.

recommendations: Lead the product on a one-time price (anchor against DaisyDisk $9.99 and DevCleaner $29 lifetime); avoid a mandatory subscription — it is the most-cited reason people abandon CleanMyMac. If recurring revenue is needed, make it optional auto-clean Pro, not a gate on core scanning.

Ship the developer-cache engine as the wedge: scan ALL projects/toolchains at once with exact known paths (Xcode DerivedData, CoreSimulator, iOS DeviceSupport, Archives, node_modules, ~/.gradle/caches, Docker, ~/.cargo, Homebrew, CocoaPods, SwiftPM, AI-tool caches). Show size + last-used date, sort by size/recency. This is the highest-confidence, most-actionable demand.

Make trust the core differentiator: a mandatory 'here is exactly what will be deleted' preview, Safe/Warning/Danger tiering, 'this regenerates automatically' reassurance copy, no account, local-only, notarized, small footprint, and an undo/archive-restore path. Consider open-sourcing the cleaning rules even if the app is paid.
Never touch source code and explicitly say so ('only known cache/build-artifact paths; source is never targeted') — and flag dependencies that break apps if deleted (npkill's ⚠️ pattern).

For non-developers, build a plain-language 'System Data explainer' that itemizes the real reclaimable culprits (local Time Machine snapshots, old iOS device backups 20-40 GB each, stale caches) with sizes, rather than a single scary opaque number.

Quantify wins in the UI and marketing the way users talk about them ('freed 80 GB: DerivedData 35 GB, Gradle 22 GB...') — the '/I freed N GB by deleting X' story is the proven viral/word-of-mouth hook.
Offer a DaisyDisk-style treemap/sunburst visualization for the 'where did my space go' job; it's the most-praised UX in this category and complements the targeted cache cleaner.

Avoid scareware/upsell marketing tone at all costs — the technical audience actively punishes 'awesomize your Mac' patronizing copy and bundled malware scanners; credibility with developers spreads to general users.

devSpace.angle: Definitive product-spec catalog of developer-related disk-space hogs on macOS: exact path(s), typical size, deletion risk tier (SAFE / REVIEW / RISKY), correct reclamation method (tool command vs delete), and the load-bearing gotcha for each. Ordered roughly by typical reclaim potential. All sizes are typical-developer-machine ranges from 2024-2026 sources; treat them as "what a scanner should expect to find," not guarantees.
devSpace.summary:
A typical macOS developer machine carries 50-200GB of reclaimable developer cruft. The biggest hogs, in order, are usually: Xcode (DerivedData + simulator runtimes + DeviceSupport + Archives, often 50-150GB combined), Docker (the Docker.raw VM disk image, 20-200GB that never auto-shrinks), node_modules sprawl across many projects (5-50GB), Android Studio AVDs + system images (often 100GB+), Rust target/ dirs (5-20GB each), and the long tail of package-manager caches (npm/yarn/pnpm/bun, Homebrew, pip/conda, Gradle/Maven, Go, Ruby, CocoaPods/SwiftPM) plus LLM model caches (HuggingFace/Ollama) and version-manager runtimes (nvm/asdf/pyenv/rbenv).

The single most important design principle for a cleanup product: distinguish "caches that fully regenerate on next use" (SAFE — just re-download/rebuild) from "artifacts that are the only copy of something" (RISKY — Archives needed for crash symbolication, AVD userdata, conda envs that take an hour to recreate). The second most important: many caches are SIP-protected or set read-only (CoreSimulator runtimes, Go module cache at 0444), so a naive `rm -rf` fails or errors — the product must use the right tool (`xcrun simctl runtime delete`, `go clean -modcache`) rather than raw deletion. Third: prune commands reclaim LOGICAL space inside a VM/store but do NOT shrink the physical file — Docker.raw is the canonical trap, where `docker system prune -a --volumes` frees space inside the Linux VM but the .raw file on the host stays bloated until you resize the disk image (which wipes everything).

Two notable 2025-2026 automation shifts the product should account for: Cargo 1.88+ now auto-GCs its global cache (~/.cargo registry), and Gradle 8+/Homebrew auto-clean on a schedule — so those caches self-limit somewhat, but per-project artifacts (target/, build/) and old-version leftovers still accumulate.

findings.point: Xcode DerivedData — biggest single quick win, always SAFE
findings.detail: Path: ~/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData/ (one subfolder per project, plus ModuleCache.noindex). Typical size: 10-50GB; never auto-pruned by Xcode. Risk: SAFE — pure build cache; Xcode regenerates on next build (first build after deletion is slow). Method: delete contents (rm -rf ~/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData/* ) or Xcode > Settings > Locations > click the arrow then trash the folder. Gotcha: delete the *contents*, not the DerivedData folder's parent; keep Xcode closed for the target project. Deleting also clears the index, so first reopen reindexes.

findings.point: Xcode CoreSimulator runtimes + devices — large, SIP-protected, must use simctl
findings.detail: Paths: ~/Library/Developer/CoreSimulator/ (Devices/ = per-AVD data; Caches/ = downloadable runtime images; runtimes mounted under /Library/Developer/CoreSimulator/ are SIP-protected). Typical size: 20-150GB; each iOS runtime is ~5-8GB. Risk: SAFE for unavailable/duplicate devices; REVIEW for runtimes you still test against (re-download is multi-GB). Method: `xcrun simctl delete unavailable` (removes orphaned devices), list runtimes with `xcrun simctl runtime list`, delete with `xcrun simctl runtime delete <id>` or `xcrun simctl runtime delete --notUsedSinceDays N`; ~/Library/Developer/CoreSimulator/Caches can be rm -rf'd. Gotcha: do NOT rm -rf the runtime bundles directly — they are SIP/mount-protected and raw deletion fails; you MUST use simctl. Quit Simulator first.

findings.point: Xcode iOS DeviceSupport — debug symbols per device/OS, mostly SAFE
findings.detail: Path: ~/Library/Developer/Xcode/iOS DeviceSupport/ (also watchOS/tvOS DeviceSupport siblings). Typical size: 10-40GB; one folder per (device, iOS build) pair, accumulates every time you connect a device on a new OS. Risk: SAFE for old iOS versions you no longer debug on real hardware; Xcode re-extracts symbols (slow, a few minutes) next time you attach that device/OS. Method: delete old version subfolders manually or rm -rf ~/Library/Developer/Xcode/iOS\ DeviceSupport/*. Gotcha: keep the folder matching your current test device's exact OS build to avoid a long re-pair; safe to nuke everything if you can tolerate one slow re-attach.

findings.point: Xcode Archives — RISKY, the one Xcode folder you should NOT blindly delete
findings.detail: Path: ~/Library/Developer/Xcode/Archives/ (dated subfolders of .xcarchive bundles). Typical size: 5-30GB. Risk: RISKY/REVIEW — .xcarchive bundles contain the dSYMs needed to symbolicate crash reports from shipped App Store builds; deleting them means you can never desymbolicate crashes for that release. Method: review in Xcode > Window > Organizer > Archives and delete only old/superseded builds; never script a blanket rm -rf. Gotcha: a cleanup tool must treat Archives differently from DerivedData — label REVIEW, surface build/version/date, and warn that dSYMs are irreplaceable if not uploaded elsewhere.

findings.point: Docker.raw VM disk image — biggest gotcha on the whole list: prune does NOT shrink it
findings.detail: Path: ~/Library/Containers/com.docker.docker/Data/vms/0/data/Docker.raw (older builds used Docker.qcow2). Typical size: 20-200GB+; grows toward the configured 'Disk image size' (default ~64GB) and never auto-shrinks. Risk: REVIEW — contents (images/containers/volumes) regenerate, but volumes may hold the ONLY copy of local DB data. Method (logical reclaim, keeps the VM): `docker system prune` (stopped containers, dangling images, networks, build cache), `docker system prune -a` (all unused images), `docker system prune -a --volumes` (also unused volumes), `docker builder prune -a` (build cache). Check first with `docker system df -v` and `docker buildx du`. Method (physical reclaim of the .raw file): Docker Desktop > Settings > Resources > Disk image size, nudge the slider and Apply & Restart — this recreates a fresh empty .raw. Gotcha: prune frees space INSIDE the Linux VM but the host-side Docker.raw stays the same size; only resizing/recreating actually returns bytes to macOS, and that wipes ALL images/containers/volumes (including local databases). For Docker.raw, host space frees within seconds after resize; qcow2 frees via a background process after minutes.

findings.point: node_modules sprawl — death by a thousand projects; npkill is the standard tool
findings.detail: Path: <every project>/node_modules/ (recursive; nested monorepo node_modules too). Typical size: 200-500MB per JS/React project, 5-50GB aggregate across a dev's repos. Risk: SAFE to delete in any project that has a lockfile (package-lock.json / yarn.lock / pnpm-lock.yaml) — reinstall reproduces it. Method: per-project `rm -rf node_modules` then reinstall; at scale use `npx npkill` (interactive TUI: scans from cwd, lists every node_modules with size, arrow+space/Del to wipe). Gotcha: a few installed *apps* ship a required node_modules — npkill flags these with a warning; never auto-delete node_modules that lacks an accompanying lockfile/package.json in its parent (could be a vendored runtime). Re-install needs network + time.

findings.point: npm / Yarn / pnpm / bun caches — global package caches, all SAFE
findings.detail: Paths: npm = ~/.npm/_cacache (and ~/.npm); Yarn Classic v1 = ~/Library/Caches/Yarn; Yarn Berry v2+ = ~/.yarn/berry/cache (or project .yarn/cache); pnpm content-addressable store = ~/Library/pnpm/store (older guides cite ~/.pnpm-store); bun = ~/.bun/install/cache. Typical size: 1-5GB each; combined with node_modules these caches reach 20-80GB. Risk: SAFE — all are redownloadable mirrors. Method: `npm cache clean --force` (force flag required); `yarn cache clean`; `pnpm store prune` (only removes store packages not referenced by ANY project — the safe, preferred approach); bun has NO built-in clean command as of early 2026, so `rm -rf ~/.bun/install/cache`. Gotcha: pnpm's store is hard-linked into projects — use `pnpm store prune`, not rm -rf, or you can break linked installs. Don't delete a project's local .yarn/cache if Yarn Berry zero-installs (committed cache) is in use.

findings.point: Android Studio: AVDs + SDK system images — can hit 100GB+, mixed risk
findings.detail: Paths: AVDs = ~/.android/avd/<name>.avd/ (userdata.img, system.img, sdcard etc.); SDK system images = ~/Library/Android/sdk/system-images/; SDK platforms/build-tools = ~/Library/Android/sdk/. Typical size: each AVD disk 6-20GB; each API system image 1.5-3GB; SDK overall 10-30GB; users report freeing 100GB+ combined with Xcode. Risk: REVIEW — deleting an AVD loses any app state/data inside it; system images re-download. Method (recommended): Android Studio > Tools > Device Manager (AVD Manager) > Delete emulator; SDK Manager > Show Package Details > untick unused System Images/platforms. Manual deletion of ~/.android/avd entries is safe only with Studio closed. Gotcha: do NOT wipe all of ~/.android — it can hold signing/debug keystores (~/.android/debug.keystore and release keys); back those up first. Wipe AVD user data via 'Wipe Data' instead of deleting the whole AVD if you just want space back.

findings.point: Rust target/ dirs + ~/.cargo — per-project target is the hog; Cargo 1.88+ auto-GCs the global cache
findings.detail: Paths: per-project ./target/ (debug+release artifacts); global registry/cache = ~/.cargo/registry/ (cache/, src/, index/); git deps = ~/.cargo/git/. Typical size: target/ 1-20GB PER project (single biggest Rust hog); ~/.cargo registry 10-100GB aggregate if many crates. Risk: SAFE — everything regenerates; target rebuilds, registry re-downloads. Method: `cargo clean` inside each project (removes that target/); for global, install cargo-cache and run `cargo cache --autoclean`, or cargo-sweep to remove only artifacts unused for N days (`cargo sweep --time 30`). Gotcha: as of Rust 1.88 (2025) Cargo has automatic GC for its global cache, so manually nuking ~/.cargo/registry is rarely needed now — but per-project target/ dirs are NOT auto-cleaned and dominate Rust disk use; a tool should scan for target/ next to Carg.toml. Safe to rm -rf ~/.cargo/registry/cache and ~/.cargo/git/db (sources re-download).

findings.point: Go module cache + build cache — module cache is read-only (0444), so rm -rf errors; use go clean
findings.detail: Paths: module cache = ~/go/pkg/mod (override via $GOMODCACHE); build/test cache = ~/Library/Caches/go-build (override via $GOCACHE). Typical size: module cache 1-10GB+; build cache 1-5GB. Risk: SAFE — both regenerate. Method: `go clean -modcache` (wipes ~/go/pkg/mod), `go clean -cache` (wipes build cache). Gotcha: files in ~/go/pkg/mod are written read-only (mode 0444) on purpose, so a plain `rm -rf ~/go/pkg/mod` fails with 'permission denied' for many users — use `go clean -modcache` (or `chmod -R +w` first). A cleanup tool must special-case Go: invoke the toolchain, not raw delete.

findings.point: Homebrew cache + old versions — auto-cleans every 30 days but cache still grows
findings.detail: Path: cache = ~/Library/Caches/Homebrew (and $(brew --cache)); old keg versions live under the Cellar (/opt/homebrew/Cellar on Apple Silicon, /usr/local/Cellar on Intel). Typical size: 2-10GB over months of installs/upgrades. Risk: SAFE — downloads are re-fetched, old versions are superseded. Method: `brew cleanup` (removes downloads + old versions >120 days), `brew cleanup --prune=all` (everything regardless of age), add `-s` to scrub even latest-version downloads, `brew cleanup -n` for dry-run; nuke download cache with `rm -rf $(brew --cache)/*`. Gotcha: since Homebrew 2.0 (2019) `brew cleanup` runs automatically every 30 days after upgrades, so it self-limits — but users who set HOMEBREW_NO_INSTALL_CLEANUP=1 accumulate indefinitely. `-s` forces re-download of current bottles next install.

findings.point: Python: conda envs (biggest), pip cache, venvs, pyenv, __pycache__
findings.detail: Paths: pip cache = ~/.cache/pip (older macOS guides also cite ~/Library/Caches/pip); conda pkg cache = ~/miniconda3/pkgs or ~/anaconda3/pkgs; conda envs = ~/miniconda3/envs/*; per-project venvs = ./venv or ./.venv; pyenv = ~/.pyenv/versions/*; bytecode = __pycache__/ + *.pyc everywhere. Typical size: forgotten conda envs 2-8GB EACH, pip cache 1-3GB, each venv 200MB-2GB, each pyenv version 50-200MB; 10-50GB+ aggregate. Risk: pip cache + __pycache__ = SAFE (regenerate). conda envs / venvs = REVIEW — they're the only copy of a resolved environment; recreating means a full reinstall (ML deps can take an hour). Method: `pip cache purge`; `conda clean --all` (dry-run first; removes only tarballs + unused extracted pkgs, does NOT touch any env's links — provably safe); delete dead venvs with rm -rf; remove __pycache__ with `find . -type d -name __pycache__ -exec rm -rf {} +`; pyenv `pyenv uninstall <ver>`. Tool: killpy (CLI) finds/deletes unused .venv/poetry/conda/pipenv/uv envs with size reporting. Gotcha: conda clean is safe (envs untouched), but DELETING an env folder is irreversible; flag envs REVIEW with last-used date.

findings.point: Java/JVM: Gradle ~/.gradle, Maven ~/.m2, Ivy ~/.ivy2 — large, mostly SAFE
findings.detail: Paths: Gradle = ~/.gradle/caches/ (modules-2 deps, build-cache-*, transforms-*) + ~/.gradle/wrapper/dists/ (downloaded Gradle distros) + ~/.gradle/daemon/; Maven local repo = ~/.m2/repository/; Ivy = ~/.ivy2/cache/. Typical size: Gradle caches+wrapper+output 10-50GB; .m2 2-10GB; .ivy2 hundreds of MB-few GB. Risk: SAFE — all re-download/rebuild. Method: per-project `./gradlew clean` (build/ output); global `rm -rf ~/.gradle/caches/build-cache-*` and `rm -rf ~/.gradle/caches/transforms-*` (safest targeted), or rm -rf ~/.gradle/caches and ~/.gradle/wrapper to go aggressive; `rm -rf ~/.m2/repository`; `rm -rf ~/.ivy2/cache`. Gotcha: Gradle 8+ auto-evicts cache entries unused >30 days — but only for the CURRENT Gradle version; caches from older Gradle versions and old wrapper dists pile up forever, so wrapper/dists is worth scanning. ~/.m2 is shared by Gradle AND Maven; only nuke it if you don't rely on Maven offline. Deleting forces a full re-resolve on next build (network + time).

findings.point: Apple dependency managers: CocoaPods, Carthage, SwiftPM — all SAFE caches
findings.detail: Paths: CocoaPods download cache = ~/Library/Caches/CocoaPods (+ ~/.cocoapods/repos spec mirror, can be large); per-project Pods/; Carthage = per-project Carthage/Build and Carthage/Checkouts; SwiftPM global cache = ~/Library/Caches/org.swift.swiftpm/ + per-project .build/. Typical size: combined 1-10GB depending on project count; SwiftPM cache 3-8GB. Risk: SAFE — every one is a mirror/build that regenerates. Method: CocoaPods `pod cache clean --all` (or per-pod `pod cache clean AFNetworking`); list with `pod cache list`; or rm -rf ~/Library/Caches/CocoaPods. Carthage: delete Carthage/Build + Carthage/Checkouts, rebuild with `carthage bootstrap`. SwiftPM: rm -rf ~/Library/Caches/org.swift.swiftpm and per-project .build/, restore with `swift package resolve`. Gotcha: per-project Pods/ and .build/ are regenerable but require re-running pod install / resolve (network); fine to delete, just costs rebuild time.

findings.point: LLM model caches: HuggingFace + Ollama — huge, REVIEW (slow/large re-download)
findings.detail: Paths: HuggingFace hub = ~/.cache/huggingface/hub (override via HF_HUB_CACHE; whole HF tree via HF_HOME), older torch/transformers at ~/.cache/torch/transformers; Ollama models = ~/.ollama/models. Typical size: Ollama 5-15GB+ (each model 1-40GB+); HF hub can be tens of GB with multiple models/datasets. Risk: REVIEW — models regenerate only via large, slow re-downloads (often many GB over the network); not 'safe' in the convenience sense. Method: Ollama — `ollama list` to see sizes, `ollama rm <model>` to remove specific models (preferred over rm -rf so the manifest stays consistent), or du -sh ~/.ollama/models/* to triage. HuggingFace — `huggingface-cli delete-cache` (interactive TUI) or `pip install huggingface_hub[cli]` then `huggingface-cli scan-cache`; manual rm -rf of ~/.cache/huggingface/hub blobs. Gotcha: these are the most expensive to re-acquire of any cache here — a cleanup product should size-rank them, show last-access, and warn about re-download cost rather than treating them like a disposable build cache.

findings.point: Version-manager runtimes: nvm, asdf, pyenv, rbenv — many old versions accumulate
findings.detail: Paths: nvm = ~/.nvm/versions/node/*; asdf = ~/.asdf/installs/<tool>/<version>/ (+ ~/.asdf/downloads); pyenv = ~/.pyenv/versions/*; rbenv = ~/.rbenv/versions/* (gems live inside each version). Typical size: each Node version 80-200MB, each pyenv Python 50-200MB; a single ~/.rbenv/versions can reach 40GB from accumulated gems across versions. Risk: REVIEW — removing a runtime deletes everything built against it (global npm tools, gems); fine if unused. Method: nvm — `nvm uninstall <ver>`, or keep only current: `cd ~/.nvm/versions/node; ls -A | grep -v $(nvm current) | xargs rm -rf`; asdf — `asdf uninstall <tool> <version>`; pyenv — `pyenv uninstall <ver>`; rbenv — `rbenv uninstall <ver>` (also run `gem cleanup` per version to drop old gem versions). Gotcha: don't delete the version another project's .nvmrc/.tool-versions/.python-version/.ruby-version pins — that silently breaks those repos. Prefer the manager's uninstall over rm -rf so shims/symlinks stay consistent.

findings.point: Ruby gems — gem cleanup removes superseded versions; rbenv versions multiply them
findings.detail: Paths: system/user gems = ~/.gem and the gems dir of each Ruby (e.g. ~/.rbenv/versions/<v>/lib/ruby/gems/...); Bundler installs may add vendor/bundle per project. Typical size: 10GB+ reclaimable across versions; a single rbenv versions tree can reach 40GB largely from gems. Risk: SAFE for old gem versions (`gem cleanup` keeps the newest of each); REVIEW for removing a whole Ruby version. Method: `gem cleanup` (removes old versions of all gems), `gem cleanup rails` (one gem), `gem cleanup --dry-run` to preview; loop `gem cleanup` across each rbenv-managed Ruby for a full sweep. Gotcha: never use sudo with rbenv (it manages permissions itself); `gem cleanup` keeps the latest version so it won't break current projects, but if a project's Gemfile.lock pins an OLD version, cleanup can remove it and force a bundle install.

findings.point: IDE caches & logs: VS Code / Cursor / JetBrains — old versions never cleaned
findings.detail: Paths: VS Code = ~/Library/Application Support/Code (Cache, CachedData, CachedExtensionVSIXs, logs, Service Worker) + ~/Library/Caches/com.microsoft.VSCode; Cursor mirrors this under .../Cursor; JetBrains caches = ~/Library/Caches/JetBrains/<Product><version>, logs = ~/Library/Logs/JetBrains, config/plugins under ~/Library/Application Support/JetBrains. Typical size: 5-30GB+ aggregate; 2-5GB per IDE, and each IDE *version* makes its own never-pruned folder. Risk: SAFE — caches/logs regenerate. Method: quit the app, then delete the Caches and Logs dirs (NOT the settings under Application Support if you want to keep config). JetBrains has built-in Help > Delete Leftover IDE Directories (auto-removes dirs untouched >180 days); Toolbox can auto-delete previous versions. Gotcha: keep ~/Library/Application Support/<IDE>/User (VS Code settings/keybindings/snippets) and JetBrains config — deleting those loses your setup; only Caches + Logs are throwaway.

findings.point: ~/Library/Developer in general — the umbrella for most Apple dev bloat
findings.detail: Path: ~/Library/Developer/ contains Xcode/ (DerivedData, Archives, iOS DeviceSupport, Products, UserData), CoreSimulator/ (devices + caches), XCTestDevices/, XCPGDevices/, Xcode/Products, and Shared/. Typical size: routinely 50-150GB on an active iOS dev machine — it is usually the #1 'System Data' culprit. Risk: MIXED — DerivedData/DeviceSupport/Caches SAFE, Archives RISKY (dSYMs), CoreSimulator runtimes need simctl. Method: treat per subfolder (see Xcode findings above); never rm -rf the whole ~/Library/Developer in one shot. Gotcha: a scanner should descend into ~/Library/Developer and classify each child by tier rather than reporting one giant number — the folder mixes throwaway caches with irreplaceable Archives.

findings.point: .DS_Store & log sprawl — tiny each, huge in count; SAFE
findings.detail: Paths: .DS_Store files in virtually every directory the Finder has visited; dev logs scattered across ~/Library/Logs, project-level *.log, npm/yarn debug logs in ~/.npm/_logs, CocoaPods/Xcode logs, etc. Typical size: each .DS_Store is a few KB but counts run into the tens of thousands; logs add up to hundreds of MB-GBs over time. Risk: SAFE — Finder regenerates .DS_Store; logs are diagnostic only. Method: `find . -name '.DS_Store' -type f -delete` (scope to a tree, or run from ~ for a full sweep); clear stale npm logs with `rm -rf ~/.npm/_logs/*`; truncate/delete old files in ~/Library/Logs. Gotcha: .DS_Store deletion is harmless but cosmetic-resetting (Finder window positions/icon arrangement reset); the real win is reducing inode/file-count noise and keeping them out of git (add to global gitignore). Don't recursively delete from / with sudo.

recommendations: Build the cleanup tool around a three-tier safety model and surface it per item: SAFE = regenerates locally with no network or trivial re-download (DerivedData, build/target caches, npm/pip/Homebrew/Gradle caches, __pycache__, .DS_Store); REVIEW = regenerates but expensively or holds the only local copy (Docker volumes, conda envs, AVD userdata, LLM models, simulator runtimes still in use); RISKY = irreplaceable (Xcode Archives/dSYMs, signing keystores under ~/.android, the only copy of unpushed data). Default-select only SAFE; require explicit confirmation for REVIEW/RISKY.

Never use a blanket `rm -rf` engine. Several targets reject or break under raw deletion: CoreSimulator runtimes are SIP/mount-protected (use `xcrun simctl runtime delete` / `xcrun simctl delete unavailable`), the Go module cache is mode-0444 read-only (use `go clean -modcache`), pnpm's store is hard-linked into projects (use `pnpm store prune`), and Ollama models should go via `ollama rm` to keep manifests consistent. Map each category to its correct tool command and fall back to rm -rf only for plain caches.

Make the Docker.raw distinction a first-class UX moment: after running `docker system prune -a --volumes` show that host disk did NOT change and explain that only resizing the Disk image size (Settings > Resources) recreates the .raw and returns bytes to macOS — and that doing so destroys all images/containers/volumes. This is the single most common source of 'I cleaned Docker but my disk is still full' confusion.

Prioritize the scanner by expected payoff: descend ~/Library/Developer (Xcode + CoreSimulator), the Docker VM disk, ~/.android + ~/Library/Android, then recursively hunt per-project artifacts that dwarf global caches — node_modules, Rust target/, Gradle build/, Python .venv, Swift .build, Pods/. Pair each found artifact with its sibling lockfile/manifest to confirm it is regenerable before offering to delete.

Account for 2025-2026 auto-cleanup so you don't double-warn on self-limiting caches: Cargo 1.88+ auto-GCs ~/.cargo, Gradle 8+ evicts entries unused >30 days (current version only), Homebrew runs cleanup every 30 days, JetBrains can auto-delete dirs unused >180 days. Focus manual-cleanup messaging on the things that genuinely never self-prune: per-project target/build dirs, old version-manager runtimes, Xcode DeviceSupport/Archives, Docker.raw, and old Gradle wrapper distributions.

For LLM model caches and version-manager runtimes, show last-access time and re-acquisition cost (download size / rebuild time), not just on-disk size — these are the items users most regret deleting. Offer 'keep current + N most-recent' presets for nvm/asdf/pyenv/rbenv and 'keep models used in last 30 days' for Ollama/HuggingFace.

safety.angle: Data-safety and trust engineering for a macOS cleaner: documented harm cases, "looks-like-junk-but-isn't" categories with exact paths, delete UX, why one-click is dangerous, how reputable tools mitigate, APFS/dataless gotchas, and concrete DO/DON'T product rules.
safety.summary: Mac cleaners cause harm in three repeatable ways: (1) deleting user data that masquerades as junk (Photos originals/derivatives, Mail "Downloads" cache misidentified as the originals, MobileSync iOS backups, sandbox containers, license/activation caches, Xcode archive dSYMs), (2) deleting things that are technically "regenerable" but expensive or destructive to lose (auth tokens, app databases under Application Support/Containers), and (3) misreading APFS so the tool fights the OS — counting purgeable space / local Time Machine snapshots as "reclaimable," failing to free space because a snapshot still references deleted files, and worst of all materializing (force-downloading) iCloud "dataless" placeholder files just by scanning them, which can silently consume gigabytes and even create an unrecoverable storage-debt state. The documented industry mitigations are a curated safety/exception database, per-OS/per-app rules, an ignore/exclusion list, defaulting risky categories OFF, never touching /System or /Library, routing deletions to Trash (not shred) by default, and not enumerating cloud-evicted files. A trustworthy cleaner must be conservative-by-default, scan without materializing, present severity tiers with a dry-run preview, route to Trash with undo, and exclude data stores by construction rather than by guesswork. Note CleanMyMac's Photo Junk is macOS 10.14-and-earlier only, so on modern macOS a cleaner should not touch the Photos library at all.

findings.point: Documented case: a cleaner deleted Photos Library originals and broke the library structure, requiring a full restore from backup
findings.detail: Apple Community reports describe CleanMyMac removing photo originals so Photos could no longer find them, breaking the non-destructive edit workflow (cannot 'revert to original'). Because the cleaner altered the library's internal package structure (e.g. removing originals and leaving edited derivatives), users could NOT simply drop missing image files back in — the only fix was restoring the entire .photoslibrary from a Time Machine backup. Apple explicitly warns that third-party apps offering to 'optimize' the Photos library will damage it: there is no supported way to purge previews/originals inside the library without corruption. Modern macOS (Catalina 10.15+) changed Photos internals; CleanMyMac's own 'Photo Junk' feature is documented as requiring macOS 10.14 or earlier, meaning on current macOS a cleaner has no safe in-library cleanup path at all. Product rule: never write to or delete inside *.photoslibrary; treat the entire package as opaque user data.

findings.point: The 'derivatives' folder inside a Photos library is NOT free junk — deleting it cripples Photos
findings.detail: The derivatives folder (inside the Photos library package, formerly ~/Pictures/Photos Library.photoslibrary/resources/derivatives) holds the rendered thumbnails/previews for every photo. Deleting it forces Photos to regenerate everything, slowing the app dramatically or preventing it from working until rebuilt — and rebuilding is not free. A naive 'large folder of image-ish files' heuristic will flag this as junk. The only genuinely-safe Photos-adjacent cache historically was the iPod/Apple-TV Photo Cache and ~/Library/Containers/com.apple.cloudphotosd (a true cache separate from the library), and newer macOS often lacks even those. Rule: a folder being large and full of regenerable assets does NOT make it safe if regeneration degrades the app.

findings.point: Mail 'Downloads' cache is safe, but the surrounding Mail data store is NOT — and the two are easy to confuse
findings.detail: Exact path of the safe-to-clear cache: ~/Library/Containers/com.apple.mail/Data/Library/Mail Downloads. This holds throwaway copies created automatically when you double-click/Quick Look/right-click an attachment; deleting them does not remove the attachment from the actual email, and explicitly-saved attachments (File > Save Attachments) go elsewhere and are untouched. HOWEVER, the rest of the Mail container (the V-numbered Mail data, Envelope Index, the actual .emlx message bodies and attachments) is the live mail store; deleting it loses locally-cached mail and can force a full re-download or break Mail. A cleaner must whitelist ONLY the 'Mail Downloads' subpath, never the parent com.apple.mail container.

findings.point: MobileSync iOS device backups look like opaque junk but are irreplaceable user data
findings.detail: Path: ~/Library/Application Support/MobileSync/Backup/. These are local iPhone/iPad backups (often tens of GB), named by UDID hash (older ones suffixed with date), so in Finder they look like meaningless gibberish folders — exactly what a junk heuristic targets. They contain the only local copy of anything on the device not synced to iCloud or re-downloadable from the App Store; deleting them = permanent loss of that backup. Because MobileSync lives UNDER Application Support, a 'clean Application Support leftovers' feature is especially dangerous here. Rule: hard-exclude MobileSync/Backup; if surfaced at all, label it as 'iOS device backup', show device name + date, default OFF, and require explicit confirmation.

findings.point: ~/Library/Application Support and ~/Library/Containers hold live app databases, not 'leftovers' — deleting them corrupts or guts apps
findings.detail: Application Support and the sandbox Containers/Group Containers folders store app databases, registration/license info, configuration, and primary user documents for sandboxed apps — not just cache. Deleting an app's Application Support subfolder while the app is still installed can corrupt it or prevent launch. Deleting a sandbox container ( ~/Library/Containers/<bundle id> ) removes user data, preferences, and documents the app relies on, causing data loss, crashes, or a reset-to-first-launch state. These are only safe to remove AFTER the parent app is uninstalled (the 'leftover removal' use case). Rule: never auto-delete anything under Application Support/Containers for an app that is still installed; tie removal to an uninstall flow, and treat sqlite/realm/leveldb/core-data stores as user data regardless of folder name.

findings.point: Deleting 'caches' can wipe license/activation state and auth tokens — technically regenerable, practically harmful
findings.detail: Adobe license info (e.g. cache.db and licensing data under /Library/Application Support/Adobe/) is sometimes stored cache-adjacent; clearing it drops the app back to trial mode and forces re-sign-in/re-entry of serials across Creative Cloud apps. Similarly, clearing an app's cache often deletes auth tokens: clearing Spotify's cache logs you out, and deleting the whole Spotify folder removes authentication tokens, forcing full re-login and breaking linked devices (Sonos, cars, speakers). The lesson: 'regenerable' is not the same as 'free to delete' — login state, license tokens, and device-link state are technically rebuildable but cost the user real friction or money. Rule: distinguish 'pure regenerable cache' (thumbnails, compiled shaders) from 'state caches' (tokens, licenses, sessions) and never lump them together; default state-bearing items OFF.

findings.point: Xcode Archives contain the dSYMs needed to symbolicate shipped-app crash reports — deleting them is irreversible
findings.detail: DerivedData (~/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData) is genuinely safe to delete: it is build output/index that fully regenerates (cost = one rebuild, 5–30 min). Archives (~/Library/Developer/Xcode/Archives) are different: each .xcarchive bundles the dSYM debug symbols for a build you shipped. If you delete the archive for a version live on TestFlight/App Store, you lose the ability to symbolicate incoming crash reports for that version, and archives CANNOT be regenerated for an already-shipped binary. A cleaner that lumps 'Xcode junk' together will silently destroy shipping infrastructure. Rule: treat DerivedData as safe-cache, but treat Archives as user data — never auto-select; if surfaced, warn about dSYM/crash-symbolication loss and default OFF.

findings.point: APFS purgeable space and local Time Machine snapshots are NOT reclaimable junk a cleaner should grab — macOS manages them automatically
findings.detail: On APFS, the large 'System'/'Other' segment in storage views is mostly purgeable space — primarily local Time Machine snapshots, which are change-catalogs (copy-on-write) not real copies. macOS auto-purges them when older than ~24h, when they grow too big, or when an app needs space. A cleaner that manually deletes snapshots fights the OS and can destroy a user's only recent local recovery point (snapshots are what let you undo bad changes). Crucially, this also explains a trust-destroying bug: after the cleaner deletes files, free space does NOT increase, because an existing snapshot still references the deleted blocks — users then think the cleaner did nothing (or lost their files). Rule: report purgeable/snapshot space transparently but never auto-delete snapshots; account for snapshots when claiming space freed, and never promise instant free-space gains.

findings.point: Scanning iCloud 'dataless' placeholder files can force-download (materialize) them — silently consuming GB and risking unrecoverable storage debt
findings.detail: With iCloud Drive + 'Optimize Mac Storage', files are evicted to dataless placeholders: metadata-only stubs whose content lives only in iCloud. Per Apple's TN3150, ordinary access — stat() and getattrlist() — materializes intermediate folders, and naively requesting full attribute sets via getattrlistbulk() (or globbing with **) triggers downloads of every file just by enumerating. The dangers for a cleaner that scans the whole disk: (a) it silently downloads gigabytes of the user's cloud data, filling the disk it was meant to clean; (b) evicted files are not locally backed up by Time Machine/Spotlight, so mistaking a stub for a deletable cache loses the only-in-cloud copy; (c) worst case, if total cloud data exceeds free space, mass materialization creates a state that 'turning Optimize back off won't fix' — an unrecoverable storage-debt scenario. Rule: detect dataless files before reading them — check NSURLUbiquitousItemDownloadingStatusKey / isUbiquitousItemKey, request only minimal attributes in getattrlistbulk so unhydrated files stay unhydrated (they report size 0 and remain dataless), skip FileProvider/iCloud-managed locations, and NEVER open or hash a file's content during a scan.

findings.point: Trash vs permanent delete: route deletions to Trash by default; shred/secure-erase is for a narrow, explicit use case and is largely meaningless on SSDs
findings.detail: Moving to Trash only removes an access point — data is recoverable until Trash is emptied (and items auto-purge after 30 days), which gives users a real undo. Permanent/shred bypasses Trash; 'Secure Shred' additionally overwrites (1-pass / 7-pass DoD / 35-pass Gutmann) so files are unrecoverable. Two product implications: (1) a cleaner should default ALL removals to Trash so mistakes are reversible, reserving permanent/secure delete for an explicit, clearly-labeled privacy action the user opts into; (2) secure-overwrite on SSDs is essentially ineffective — wear-leveling writes the 'overwrite' to a new block, leaving the original recoverable — so don't advertise multi-pass shredding as a guarantee on modern Macs, and don't waste write cycles. Rule: Trash-by-default + visible undo; treat 'permanent' as a separate, confirmed, well-explained mode.

findings.point: Why 'one-click clean everything' is dangerous and largely unnecessary on modern macOS
findings.detail: One-click cleaners aggregate many heuristics and execute them without item-level review, so a single false positive (a misidentified cache, a Photos derivative, a license token) is deleted with everything else and the user never sees it coming — and review-then-clean is exactly the safety valve that prevents this. Critics note macOS already self-manages most of what cleaners target: APFS has immutable system volumes (since Catalina), automatic purgeable-space/cache eviction, and sandboxing that blocks user-space apps from touching core system dirs — so aggressive cleaning offers little real gain while adding risk. Many 'junk' detectors also inflate findings (reports of cleaners flagging 1000+ 'issues' on healthy Macs; analyses finding the bulk of flagged items were system-protected, app runtime assets, or already auto-cleaned), which both erodes trust and pressures users into destructive bulk actions. Rule: no blind one-click delete — scan is one-click, cleaning requires review (or at minimum, only the conservative tier auto-runs).

findings.point: How reputable tools mitigate: curated safety database, per-OS/per-app exception rules, hard-protected paths, ignore lists, and risky categories OFF by default
findings.detail: CleanMyMac's documented safety model is the reference pattern: (1) a continuously-updated Safety Database of cleaning rules + exceptions tailored to specific macOS versions and specific apps, so removal decisions are rule-driven not heuristic-guessed; (2) hard-protected locations it refuses to enter or delete — it won't touch /Library or /System/Library, and it blocks dropping critical folders (e.g. Documents) into the Shredder even if the user tries; (3) by default it only offers automatically-generated system/app data and removes no personal files unless the user explicitly chooses; (4) user-extensible Ignore Lists per module (System Junk, Mail Attachments, Uninstaller, Duplicates, etc.) so users can permanently exclude paths; (5) risky categories (e.g. local iCloud photo copies) are NOT selected by default and are labeled with the consequence ('you'll need internet to view these again'). For pricing/positioning context (2025): CleanMyMac Basic 1-Mac ~$9.95/mo, ~$47.50/yr, ~$119.95 one-time; Plus 1-Mac ~$15.95/mo, ~$71.40/yr, ~$195.95 one-time. Rule: ship a maintained allowlist/denylist keyed by OS version + bundle ID, hard-exclude system trees, default-OFF anything that needs network or loses state, and make exclusions user-editable and sticky.

recommendations: DO scan read-only and metadata-only: enumerate with getattrlistbulk requesting MINIMAL attributes, never open/read/hash file content during a scan, and check NSURLUbiquitousItemDownloadingStatusKey / isUbiquitousItemKey first so iCloud dataless files stay unhydrated. DON'T let a scan materialize cloud files or walk FileProvider/iCloud-managed paths.

DO maintain a curated, versioned safety database keyed by macOS version + app bundle ID (allowlist of known-safe cache paths, denylist of data stores). DON'T classify by heuristics like 'large folder of regenerable-looking files' or 'gibberish folder names' — that is exactly how MobileSync backups and Photos derivatives get destroyed.

DON'T ever touch: /System, /System/Library, /Library, the entire *.photoslibrary package (originals AND derivatives), ~/Library/Application Support/MobileSync/Backup, ~/Library/Developer/Xcode/Archives (dSYMs), or any sqlite/realm/leveldb/core-data store. DO hard-exclude these by construction, not by user vigilance.

DO only clean a known cache SUBPATH, never its parent: e.g. allow ~/Library/Containers/com.apple.mail/Data/Library/Mail Downloads but never the parent com.apple.mail container; allow DerivedData but never Archives.

DON'T delete app data for an installed app. DO gate Application Support / Containers / Group Containers removal behind an explicit uninstall flow, and only remove leftovers for apps that are already gone.

DO separate 'pure regenerable cache' (thumbnails, shader caches, DerivedData) from 'state caches' (auth tokens, license/activation files, sessions) and default the state-bearing ones OFF with a plain-language consequence ('you will be signed out / need to re-enter your license').
DON'T do blind one-click delete. DO make Scan one-click but require a reviewable, item-level dry-run preview before any deletion; show exactly which paths, sizes, and the consequence per item.

DO present severity tiers: a conservative default tier (truly disposable caches/logs/trash) vs. an advanced tier that is opt-in, per-item, and consequence-labeled. DON'T let bulk 'select all' silently include advanced/risky items.

DO route every deletion to the Trash by default with a working Undo, and account for the 30-day Trash window. DON'T permanently delete or 'shred' by default; make secure-erase a separate, explicitly-confirmed mode, and don't advertise multi-pass overwrite as a guarantee on SSDs (wear-leveling defeats it).
DO give users a persistent, editable Ignore/Exclusion list per category, and never re-surface an excluded path. DON'T reset exclusions on update.
DON'T touch APFS purgeable space or local Time Machine snapshots — macOS auto-manages them and they are the user's local undo. DO surface them read-only as 'managed by macOS'.

DO account for snapshots/copy-on-write when reporting 'space freed': verify actual free-space delta and never promise instant gains, because a snapshot can still reference just-deleted blocks. DON'T claim X GB recovered if the blocks are still referenced.

DO require Full Disk Access transparently and explain why, log every action to an auditable, exportable history, and provide a one-click 'restore from Trash' for the last operation. DON'T act on paths the user can't see or review.

macosTech.angle: Technical feasibility and recommended architecture for a native SwiftUI macOS disk cleaner distributed outside the Mac App Store (Developer ID + notarized), covering disk-usage measurement, APFS purgeable/snapshot accounting, TCC/Full Disk Access, sandbox tradeoffs, safe delete, node_modules scanning, running shell tools, security-scoped bookmarks, and SMAppService helpers.
macosTech.summary: A full-disk cleaner CANNOT be App-Sandboxed and still do its job — this is the single most important architectural fact, and it dictates everything else. Ship as a non-sandboxed, Developer ID-signed, Hardened-Runtime, notarized app, and request Full Disk Access (TCC service kTCCServiceSystemPolicyAllFiles) which the sandbox would otherwise block. CleanMyMac itself ships the full-featured product outside the App Store for exactly this reason; its App Store build is feature-limited by the sandbox. For fast scanning, FileManager's URL enumerator with prefetched resource keys is the pragmatic high-performance choice (Foundation has heavily optimized the layer beneath it), while the genuinely fastest approach is the getattrlistbulk syscall with a work-stealing thread pool (~6.4x faster than du). Report "real" free space via volumeAvailableCapacityForImportantUsageKey (which accounts for purgeable space), not raw statfs/df. Delete via FileManager.trashItem(at:resultingItemURL:) — never removeItem. Run docker/brew via Process with absolute paths, never a shell string. Use SMAppService only if you need root operations. Detecting FDA has no official API — you must attempt to read a known protected file and check for EPERM/EACCES.

findings.point: A full-disk cleaner CANNOT be App-Sandboxed — ship non-sandboxed, Developer ID-signed, Hardened-Runtime, notarized. This is confirmed and load-bearing.
findings.detail: App Sandbox confines an app to its container and grants file access only through user-selected files (NSOpenPanel) or temporary-exception entitlements; it is mandatory for the Mac App Store but OPTIONAL for Developer ID distribution. Full Disk Access (FDA) and the sandbox are mutually exclusive — 'Full Disk Access won't work with sandboxed apps because of the sandbox.' A cleaner that must enumerate ~/Library/Caches, ~/Library/Developer (Xcode), /private/var, other users' areas, etc. cannot do so sandboxed. Proof by existence: MacPaw ships the full CleanMyMac outside the App Store; the Mac App Store build exists but 'Apple's technical restrictions mean that it may not have the full range of features available when you buy CleanMyMac directly from MacPaw' — i.e. the sandbox strips features. Recommended posture: App Sandbox OFF, Hardened Runtime ON (required for notarization), notarize with the Developer ID Application certificate. Only add Hardened Runtime exception entitlements you actually need (e.g. com.apple.security.cs.disable-library-validation only if loading 3rd-party unsigned frameworks; avoid allow-unsigned-executable-memory/allow-jit unless required).

findings.point: Fast disk-usage scanning: FileManager URL enumerator (with prefetched keys) is the pragmatic best; getattrlistbulk + thread pool is the genuine speed ceiling (~6.4x faster than du). du is slow because it does one lstat() per file.
findings.detail: du / naive scanners issue 400k+ individual lstat() syscalls — syscall overhead dominates. The fastest known macOS approach (Healey's 'dumac') calls the getattrlistbulk syscall, which batches readdir+stat into a 128KB buffer returning dozens-hundreds of entries per call; on a 409,500-file benchmark it hit 521ms vs du's 3.33s (6.4x) and diskus's 1.34s (2.58x), with syscalls ~91% of runtime. Best concurrency was a work-stealing pool (Rayon-style), NOT spawning a thread per call — that cut syscalls in half and context switches ~80% (1.2M->235k). Inode dedup (for hardlinks/clones) needs sharded locks keyed on (inode>>8)%N because APFS issues sequential inodes. BUT: in Tempel/Tsai's macOS tests, Foundation's high-level enumeratorAtURL actually beat raw fts_read/getattrlistbulk on local HFS+/APFS because 'the API underneath was SPECIFICALLY added to make the Foundation/CoreFoundation layer faster.' fts_open/fts_read/fts_close generally beats readdir/contentsOfDirectory but loses to getattrlistbulk on network volumes. APFS directory enumeration is ~5-6x slower than HFS+ and got ~15% slower again on Mojave+. RECOMMENDED: FileManager.enumerator(at:includingPropertiesForKeys:[.fileSizeKey,.totalFileAllocatedSizeKey,.isDirectoryKey,.fileResourceTypeKey], options:[.skipsHiddenFiles? no — cleaners want hidden],...) streaming results via AsyncStream with ~50ms UI-update throttling (the pattern MacDirStat uses). Drop to a getattrlistbulk C shim only if you need the absolute floor. Use totalFileAllocatedSizeKey (on-disk blocks) not fileSizeKey (logical) for accurate 'space reclaimed' numbers.

findings.point: Report 'real' free space with URLResourceValues key volumeAvailableCapacityForImportantUsageKey, NOT raw statfs/df — that key accounts for purgeable space the OS will reclaim on demand.
findings.detail: macOS layers a space-management system (the CacheDelete subsystem) over APFS that marks content (caches, Time Machine local snapshots) 'purgeable' and frees it automatically when space is needed; it is NOT counted as used. df/statfs and even Finder lag reality — Finder caches values and doesn't re-fetch after CacheDelete recomputes. Use URL(fileURLWithPath:'/').resourceValues(forKeys:) with: volumeAvailableCapacityForImportantUsageKey (10.13+, Int64 — space available for important resources, accounting for purgeable; what to show as 'free'), volumeAvailableCapacityForOpportunisticUsageKey (10.13+, safer/more conservative for opportunistic downloads), volumeAvailableCapacityKey (legacy, ignores purgeable), volumeTotalCapacityKey. Gate on volumeSupportsVolumeSizesKey first. For local APFS snapshots specifically: enumerate with `tmutil listlocalsnapshots /` (Time Machine creates hourly local snapshots — the main purgeable contributor); note listlocalsnapshots does NOT report per-snapshot reclaimable size. df reflects actively-allocated storage only after snapshots are deleted. Product implication: don't promise 'X GB free' from one number — distinguish truly free vs purgeable vs snapshot-held, and surface snapshots as a separate reclaim category (DaisyDisk does this).

findings.point: Full Disk Access uses TCC service identifier kTCCServiceSystemPolicyAllFiles. There is NO official API to query or trigger it — you detect by attempting to read a known protected file and request by deep-linking the user to System Settings.
findings.detail: FDA is the TCC service 'kTCCServiceSystemPolicyAllFiles'. Apple provides no public API to read grant status (reading TCC.db directly is unsupported and not considered API). DETECTION pattern (what CleanMyMac/MacPaw's open-source PermissionsKit does): attempt to read several protected files and treat success as 'granted', checking multiple to avoid false negatives — files used: ~/Library/Safari/Bookmarks.plist, ~/Library/Safari/CloudTabs.db, /Library/Application Support/com.apple.TCC/TCC.db, /Library/Preferences/com.apple.TimeMachine.plist. open()/Data(contentsOf:) returning -1 with errno EPERM/EACCES => not granted; valid data => granted. Reading these does NOT itself raise a TCC prompt. Reliability caveat: the test can false-negative due to unrelated dir permissions (700 vs 755), so test several files. REQUEST pattern: there is no programmatic grant and NO completion callback — open the pane directly with URL 'x-apple.systempreferences:com.apple.preference.security?Privacy_AllFiles' (NSWorkspace.shared.open) and then POLL the detection check for the change. macOS Ventura+ may require the user to toggle/relaunch. CleanMyMac's in-app copy directs users: 'Open System Settings, click Privacy & Security, then select Full Disk Access' and grants to multiple components (main app + Health Monitor + Menu helper). Each separately-signed helper/login item needs its own FDA grant.

findings.point: Safe delete: use FileManager.trashItem(at:resultingItemURL:) exclusively. Never removeItem(at:) for user-facing cleanup.
findings.detail: trashItem(at:resultingItemURL:) moves a file to the user's Trash (recoverable, one-click restore) and returns the resulting Trash URL via an autoreleasing out-parameter (in Swift: `var trashURL: NSURL?; try fm.trashItem(at: url, resultingItemURL: &trashURL)`). This is the correct, reversible primitive for a cleaner — it preserves an undo path and matches user expectations. removeItem(at:)/removeItem(atPath:) is permanent and should be reserved (if ever) for transient app-internal temp files the user never sees. Note: items in the system Trash still occupy disk until the user empties it, so 'space reclaimed' messaging should account for that (offer an explicit 'Empty Trash' step or report 'moved to Trash'). On a non-sandboxed FDA app, trashItem works across the whole disk; trashing system-protected or other-user files may still fail with permission errors that you must surface gracefully.

findings.point: node_modules whole-disk scanning: the key optimization is to PRUNE — once a node_modules directory is found, record its size and do NOT descend into it (no recursing into nested node_modules). npkill is the reference implementation.
findings.detail: npkill scans the disk for every node_modules dir, reports size, and offers selective deletion; its performance comes from low-level traversal and treating each node_modules as a discrete target rather than continuing to descend. The critical algorithmic point for your scanner: when the enumerator hits a directory named 'node_modules', size it (sum totalFileAllocatedSize of contents) and skip its entire subtree — this avoids the pathological case of double-counting and re-walking deeply nested node_modules/.../node_modules. With FileManager.DirectoryEnumerator you call enumerator.skipDescendants() upon matching. Also pre-prune known-huge irrelevant trees (e.g., skip /System, /Volumes/<network>, .Trash, and ideally let users exclude paths — npkill supports an exclude list of comma-separated, quoted dirs). Same pattern generalizes to other dev caches worth targeting: ~/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData, ~/Library/Caches, ~/.gradle, ~/.cargo, Docker.raw, .venv, target/, build/, Pods/. Scanning from '/' is expensive; default to $HOME and common dev roots, with full-disk opt-in.

findings.point: Running docker/brew from Swift: use Foundation Process with an ABSOLUTE executableURL and an arguments array — never pass a shell command string. Don't assume $PATH; Homebrew binaries live at /opt/homebrew/bin (Apple Silicon) or /usr/local/bin (Intel). These cannot run from a sandboxed app.
findings.detail: Use Process (the modern NSTask): set process.executableURL = URL(fileURLWithPath: '/opt/homebrew/bin/brew'), process.arguments = ['cleanup','--prune=all'], wire stdout/stderr to Pipe(), call try process.run(), read pipe.fileHandleForReading.readDataToEndOfFile(), then process.waitUntilExit() and check terminationStatus. SECURITY rules: (1) Never use /bin/sh -c with an interpolated string — pass discrete arguments to avoid shell injection. (2) Resolve absolute paths; a GUI app launched from Finder has a minimal PATH that usually lacks /opt/homebrew/bin, so locate brew/docker explicitly (Apple Silicon /opt/homebrew/bin, Intel /usr/local/bin; docker CLI often /usr/local/bin/docker or ~/.docker symlinks). (3) docker/brew run as the user — no root needed; do NOT shell out for things with native APIs (free space, trashing). (4) A SANDBOXED app cannot spawn these — 'docker commands may be outside of the sandbox' — reinforcing the non-sandboxed design. Avoid AuthorizationExecuteWithPrivileges/STPrivilegedTask (deprecated since 10.7). If you genuinely need root (rare for a cleaner — e.g., clearing system-owned caches), use an SMAppService daemon + XPC, not privileged shell-outs.

findings.point: Security-scoped bookmarks are primarily a SANDBOX mechanism. A non-sandboxed FDA cleaner generally does NOT need them — but plain bookmarkData() (without .withSecurityScope) is still useful to remember user-selected folders across launches.
findings.detail: Security-scoped bookmarks (url.bookmarkData(options: .withSecurityScope,...), resolve with URL(resolvingBookmarkData:options:[.withSecurityScope,.withoutUI],...), gate access with startAccessingSecurityScopedResource()/stopAccessingSecurityScopedResource()) exist to grant a SANDBOXED app persistent access beyond its container after the user picks a path via NSOpenPanel. They require the com.apple.security.files.user-selected.read-write entitlement plus com.apple.security.files.bookmarks.app-scope/document-scope. For a NON-sandboxed FDA app these are unnecessary for access (FDA already grants disk-wide reads); you'd use ordinary url.bookmarkData() (no security scope) purely to persist 'last scanned folders' robustly across renames/moves. Note Apple has had sandbox-escape CVEs in scoped bookmarks (CVE-2025-31191), another reason the non-sandboxed model is simpler here. If you ever DID ship a sandboxed companion (App Store SKU), scoped bookmarks + NSOpenPanel('Grant access to this folder') become mandatory and are the only way to reach arbitrary folders.

findings.point: SMAppService (macOS 13+) is the modern replacement for SMJobBless — needed only if your cleaner performs ROOT-level operations. For a user-space cleaner with FDA, you likely don't need a privileged helper at all.
findings.detail: SMAppService (macOS 13+) registers helpers that live INSIDE the app bundle (Contents/Library/LaunchDaemons/<plist>, Contents/Library/LaunchAgents/, Contents/MacOS/<helper executable>) rather than installing into /Library/PrivilegedHelperTools. Factory methods: SMAppService.daemon(plistName:), .agent(plistName:), .loginItem(identifier:); lifecycle: try service.register() / service.unregister(); status enum: .notRegistered/.enabled/.requiresApproval/.notFound. A daemon (root) registration triggers an admin auth prompt and the user must approve in System Settings > General > Login Items & Extensions; agents/login items just need toggling. App+helper must share a Developer ID team prefix and be notarized; the helper is code-signed and you communicate via XPC (NSXPCConnection). WHEN a cleaner needs this: clearing system-owned caches (/Library/Caches, /private/var/folders system entries), pruning files owned by root, or scheduled background cleanup. WHEN it doesn't: trashing user files, dev caches (~/Library, node_modules, DerivedData), and free-space reporting — all run fine in the main user-space process with FDA. Recommend: ship WITHOUT a privileged helper for v1; add an SMAppService daemon later only for specific root-only categories, and keep it minimal to ease notarization (Xcode archiving rejects bundles with stray embedded executables unless the helper is properly set up).

findings.point: Concrete sign/notarize/staple pipeline for Developer ID distribution, plus market pricing reference points.
findings.detail: Build with Hardened Runtime ON, App Sandbox OFF. Sign deepest-first then the app/dmg with the Developer ID Application cert: codesign --force --options runtime --timestamp --entitlements App.entitlements --sign 'Developer ID Application: Name (TEAMID)' <bundle>; verify: codesign -vvv --deep --strict <bundle> and spctl -a -vvv <bundle>. Notarize (notarytool, the modern tool; altool is retired): xcrun notarytool submit MyApp.dmg --apple-id <id> --password <app-specific-password> --team-id <TEAMID> --wait (or use a stored keychain profile via --keychain-profile). On success staple so it works offline: xcrun stapler staple MyApp.dmg (and staple the .app before packaging the dmg). Distribute the stapled DMG. Pricing benchmarks for a product spec: CleanMyMac Basic $9.95/mo or $47.50/yr, or one-time $119.95; Plus $15.95/mo / $71.40/yr / one-time $195.95 (subscription-led, Developer-ID/notarized, sold direct off macpaw.com). DaisyDisk is a one-time $9.99, 1 license for up to 5 personal Macs, 30-day money-back — the 'pay-once utility' counterpoint. This frames the two viable GTM models: subscription (CleanMyMac) vs one-time license (DaisyDisk).

recommendations: Ship NON-sandboxed: App Sandbox OFF, Hardened Runtime ON, Developer ID Application signature, notarytool submit --wait + stapler staple. A sandboxed full-disk cleaner is technically impossible (FDA and sandbox are mutually exclusive) — confirmed by CleanMyMac's feature-limited App Store build.

Architecture: a single user-space SwiftUI app process does 95% of the work (scan, size, trash, report). Add an SMAppService root daemon (XPC) ONLY later for system-owned caches. Do not build a privileged helper for v1.

Scanning engine: FileManager.enumerator(at:includingPropertiesForKeys:[.totalFileAllocatedSizeKey,.isDirectoryKey,.fileResourceTypeKey]) streamed through an AsyncStream with ~50ms UI throttle. Use totalFileAllocatedSize (on-disk blocks) for reclaim figures. Drop to a getattrlistbulk C shim + work-stealing pool only if you need the ~6x-over-du ceiling.

node_modules / dev caches: prune-on-match — on hitting a target dir (node_modules, DerivedData, .gradle, target, Pods), size it and call skipDescendants() to avoid re-walking nested copies. Default scan root = $HOME; full-disk is opt-in with a user-editable exclude list.

Free-space reporting: use volumeAvailableCapacityForImportantUsageKey (accounts for purgeable) as the headline 'free' number; never statfs/df raw. Surface APFS local snapshots (tmutil listlocalsnapshots /) and purgeable as separate, clearly-labeled reclaim categories.
Deletion: FileManager.trashItem(at:resultingItemURL:) only — preserves undo. Track resulting Trash URLs for an in-app 'Restore' and a separate explicit 'Empty Trash to reclaim space' action.

FDA UX: detect by test-reading several protected files (e.g. ~/Library/Safari/Bookmarks.plist, /Library/Preferences/com.apple.TimeMachine.plist) and treating EPERM/EACCES as 'not granted'; request by opening x-apple.systempreferences:com.apple.preference.security?Privacy_AllFiles and polling status (there is no callback). Mirror CleanMyMac's onboarding copy and grant each signed helper separately.

Shell-outs (docker/brew): Foundation Process with absolute executableURL (/opt/homebrew/bin on Apple Silicon, /usr/local/bin on Intel) and an arguments array — never /bin/sh -c with a string. These only work because the app is non-sandboxed.

GTM framing: decide subscription (CleanMyMac: $9.95/mo, $47.50/yr, $119.95 once) vs one-time license (DaisyDisk: $9.99, 5 Macs). A notarized direct-download DMG with a license-key activation fits either.

naming.angle: Positioning, pricing, and naming for a one-time-purchase, developer-focused Mac cleaner from a solo studio (Emotive Impact), wedged against bloated subscription incumbents (CleanMyMac) and the free open-source crowd.
naming.summary: The market splits cleanly into three camps and leaves an open lane in the middle. (1) Subscription incumbents: CleanMyMac is ~$39.95/yr for one Mac (legacy one-time licenses run ~$89.95+), and is widely criticized by power users as a bloated background-process suite that nags about RAM/malware and duplicates what macOS already does. (2) Cheap one-time generalists: DaisyDisk at $9.99 (visualizer only, doesn't clean caches) and Sensei at $59 one-time / $29/yr (3 Macs). (3) A fast-growing free/open-source developer-cleaner niche — DevCleaner, Pearcleaner, PureMac, MacSai, Cruft, Brisk — that proves developers actively want a focused, transparent, no-subscription, dev-cache-aware tool but mostly ships unpolished, abandonment-prone freeware (Pearcleaner development paused end of 2025). The wedge: a polished, paid-once, developer-native cleaner that targets the 60-300GB of dev bloat generic cleaners ignore (Xcode DerivedData, node_modules, Docker, Cargo, Gradle/Maven, simulators, IDE caches), with zero subscription, zero background daemons, and zero telemetry. Recommended price band: $25-39 one-time, single tier, ~3-Mac license. NOTE: several obvious names are already taken — "Cruft" (cruft.app, exact same dev-cache positioning), "Brisk" (GitHub Mac cleaner), "Scrub" and "Pry" (existing App Store apps), "MacSweep"/"Tidy Up Mac" (exist). The 10 names below were filtered against those collisions; do USPTO + domain checks before committing.

findings.point: CleanMyMac is now subscription-first at ~$39.95/yr (1 Mac); legacy one-time licenses are ~$89.95-$119.95 and exclude future major upgrades
findings.detail: MacPaw lists CleanMyMac annual at ~$39.95/yr for one Mac (~$3.33/mo equivalent), ~$54.95/yr for 2 Macs, ~$89.95/yr for 5 Macs. Older one-time/lifetime tiers were quoted at $89.95-$119.95 (Basic) and up to $195.95 (Plus), but the one-time price explicitly 'may not include additional major updates and features.' This is the price anchor and the thing power users resent paying recurringly 'to delete files.' Your one-time price undercuts this dramatically and removes the recurring-fee objection entirely.

findings.point: Power-user / developer distrust of CleanMyMac is real and specific: bloated background processes, nagging upsells, suspected false-positive malware alerts, duplicating native macOS features
findings.detail: Documented criticism: CleanMyMac 'lives in the menu bar constantly,' 'nags users about RAM usage and asks to scan for malware,' runs background Health Monitor processes, and is seen as duplicating macOS Storage/Activity Monitor. Apple Community threads report false malware alarms (suspected upsell tactic) and system freezes after updates. This is your messaging ammunition — position explicitly AGAINST the daemon/nag/upsell model: launches when you open it, does its job, quits.

findings.point: A dedicated developer-bloat niche exists and is validated: generic cleaners miss 60-300GB of dev caches across ~20+ ecosystems
findings.detail: Concrete dev-bloat targets generic cleaners ignore, with real paths/sizes: Xcode DerivedData ~/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData (10-50GB), iOS Simulators (20-150GB), node_modules (10-60GB), Docker images/volumes/Docker.raw (10-50GB), Rust cargo target/ (5-30GB), Python venv/conda (5-20GB), Gradle/Maven (3-15GB), Homebrew cache (2-10GB), VS Code/JetBrains caches (2-10GB). DevCleaner ships scanners for 23 ecosystems. THIS is the sharpest wedge — be the cleaner that natively understands dev tools, not a generic junk-sweeper with a 'developer' checkbox.

findings.point: POSITIONING WEDGE (recommended one-liner): 'Reclaim 50+GB of dev-tool bloat in one click — buy it once, no subscription, no background daemons, no nags.'
findings.detail: Tighter alternatives to A/B test: (a) 'The Mac cleaner that actually understands your dev tools — Xcode, node_modules, Docker, simulators. One-time price, runs only when you open it.' (b) 'CleanMyMac for people who hate CleanMyMac: focused, fast, paid once.' The wedge combines three orthogonal advantages competitors can't all claim simultaneously: developer-native scanners (beats CleanMyMac/DaisyDisk), one-time price (beats CleanMyMac subscription), and polish + maintenance + safety (beats the free OSS tools, which are abandonment-prone — Pearcleaner's own dev paused work end of 2025). Lead with the dev angle because the free OSS crowd validated demand but left a quality/trust gap a paid solo studio can fill.

findings.point: PRICING (recommended): $29 one-time, single tier, ~3-Mac license, with a free scan / paid clean trial. Acceptable band $25-39.
findings.detail: Competitive anchors: DaisyDisk $9.99 one-time (5 Macs, but visual-only — doesn't clean caches); Sensei $59 one-time or $29/yr (3 Macs); VaultSort $24.99 one-time vs $39.95/yr; CleanMyMac $39.95/yr. The free OSS tools (DevCleaner, Pearcleaner, PureMac, MacSai) set the floor at $0, so the paid pitch must be polish + safety + dev-native depth + active maintenance. $29 one-time sits below CleanMyMac's first-year subscription, reads as a 'fair, honest' price to the anti-subscription crowd, beats Sensei's $59 entry, and is high enough to signal quality over the $9.99 toys. Match DaisyDisk/Sensei's multi-Mac generosity (3 seats) since developers commonly run a laptop + desktop. Avoid a subscription entirely — it would forfeit the entire positioning. If recurring revenue is later needed, use paid major-version upgrades (the Sketch/Sublime model), never a recurring license.

findings.point: NAME 1 — Husk
findings.detail: Rationale: a husk is the empty shell left after the kernel is removed — evokes stripping away dead weight/bloat, short and evocative like Vlume/Tapio. .com likely taken (common word) but huskapp.com / gethusk.com / husk.dev plausible. Trademark risk: MEDIUM — generic English word, several unrelated 'Husk' software products exist (e.g. a SaaS/CSS tool); clears as a Mac-cleaner mark but do a USPTO class-9/42 search.

findings.point: NAME 2 — Strato
findings.detail: Rationale: from 'stratum/strata' (layers of accumulated cruft) and clean stratosphere/airy space; brandable two-syllable like LoudMix/Mixly. .com almost certainly taken (Strato AG is a large German hosting company) — use trystrato.com / strato.app. Trademark risk: HIGH on bare 'Strato' — STRATO is a well-known registered hosting/IT brand in the EU. Recommend a modifier or coinage (Stratoclean, Stratos) only after counsel; listed for sound, flagged as risky.

findings.point: NAME 3 — Vacuo
