findings.detail: Rationale: Latin root of 'vacuum/empty' — implies reclaiming empty space; invented-feel, short, family-consistent. No Mac cleaner found under this name in searches. .com plausibly available or cheap (vacuo.app / vacuo.dev strong). Trademark risk: LOW-MEDIUM — 'Vacuo' appears as a brand in unrelated fields (some beverage/industrial uses internationally); software class likely clear, verify USPTO.

findings.point: NAME 4 — Vacate
findings.detail: Rationale: 'vacate the space' — clear cleaning/space verb, confident and memorable. No Mac cleaner found under this name (search surfaced only Tidy Up / Washing Machine for the adjacent 'reclaim' query). .com likely registered (real English word) — vacate.app / getvacate.com fallback. Trademark risk: MEDIUM — common word, used in legal/property SaaS contexts; software-utility class likely clear.

findings.point: NAME 5 — Sweepr
findings.detail: Rationale: vowel-dropped 'sweeper' (Flickr/Tumblr style), directly hints at cleaning, short and brandable. CAUTION: an Irish customer-support automation company named 'Sweepr' (sweepr.com) exists — different category but same spelling. .com taken; sweepr.app / sweepr.dev possible. Trademark risk: MEDIUM-HIGH due to the existing Sweepr Technologies mark — consider Sweepo/Sweepkit instead. Note: avoid plain 'Sweep'/'MacSweep' — MacSweep.app already exists.

findings.point: NAME 6 — Pareo / Pare
findings.detail: Rationale: 'to pare down' = trim away excess — precise metaphor for cleaning bloat; 'Pareo' adds a brandable vowel ending matching Tapio. 'Pare' alone is a dictionary word (harder TM/domain); 'Pareo' is more ownable (note: 'pareo' is also a sarong garment — minor semantic clash, no software collision found). pareo.app / pare.dev plausible. Trademark risk: LOW-MEDIUM for software class.

findings.point: NAME 7 — Derelict / Derel
findings.detail: Rationale: nods directly to Xcode 'DerivedData' (the #1 dev-bloat target) while meaning 'abandoned/leftover' — the orphaned caches you delete. Strong insider wink for developers. 'Derel' is a cleaner coinage; full 'Derelict' is evocative but long. derel.app / derelict.dev likely available. Trademark risk: LOW — uncommon as a software name; verify.

findings.point: NAME 8 — Reclaim / Reclaimr
findings.detail: Rationale: 'reclaim your disk space' is the literal job; instantly communicates value. CAUTION: very crowded — Intego's Washing Machine has a 'Reclaim' cycle, and Reclaim.ai is a well-known calendar startup (reclaim.com/.ai taken). Use the vowel-dropped 'Reclaimr' for ownability + family fit (Mixly/Vlume style). reclaimr.app possible. Trademark risk: HIGH on bare 'Reclaim', MEDIUM on 'Reclaimr'.

findings.point: NAME 9 — Spano / Spaze
findings.detail: Rationale: coined from 'space' (the thing you reclaim) — invented, .com-plausible, phonetically in-family with Tapio/Mixly. No Mac cleaner found under either spelling. spano.app / spaze.app likely available; 'Spaze' is an existing minor brand in a few markets so 'Spano' is safer. Trademark risk: LOW for software; verify spelling collisions.

findings.point: NAME 10 — Cairn
findings.detail: Rationale: a cairn is a deliberate stack of stones — flips 'pile of junk' into 'curated, intentional stack,' implying safe/considered cleaning (anti-reckless-delete trust angle, which matters since users fear cleaners breaking their setup). Short, evocative, distinctly not a generic 'clean' word — strong brand-family fit. cairn.app / getcairn.com plausible (cairn.com likely taken — common word, used by Cairn Energy/Cairn Homes). Trademark risk: MEDIUM — multiple unrelated 'Cairn' companies (energy, publishing); software-utility class likely clear, verify USPTO.

findings.point: NAMES TO AVOID — confirmed collisions in the exact category
findings.detail: Do NOT use: 'Cruft' (cruft.app is a private/native Mac developer-cache cleaner with the EXACT positioning you'd claim — direct collision); 'Brisk' (GitHub.com/GhassanKY/BRISK is a native macOS app cleaner / leftover scanner); 'Scrub' (multiple App Store apps incl. Scrub Web Browser, Scrub EXIF tool); 'Pry' (App Store app id846195114); 'MacSweep' (macsweep.app exists); 'Tidy Up' (Tidy Up Mac exists); 'Mole' (tw93/Mole terminal cleaner); 'Sensei'/'DaisyDisk'/'CleanMyMac'/'Pearcleaner'/'DevCleaner'/'PureMac'/'MacSai' (all live competitors). 'Lumber' is heavily used in unrelated App Store apps.

findings.point: Go-to-market note: trust and safety are the conversion lever, not feature count
findings.detail: Across the OSS alternatives the repeated promises are 'zero telemetry,' 'never touches system files,' 'shows exact paths and sizes so you can deselect before deleting,' and 'notarized.' For a paid app the trust bar is higher: ship Apple-notarized, document exactly what each scanner deletes (with paths), make every deletion reviewable/undoable, and state plainly 'no analytics, no account, no daemon.' That directly answers the developer distrust that pushed people off CleanMyMac, and justifies a paid price over free OSS by adding maintenance + safety guarantees the abandoned free tools can't promise.

recommendations: Positioning one-liner to ship: 'Reclaim 50+GB of dev-tool bloat in one click. Buy once, no subscription, no background daemons, no nags.' Lead the landing page with concrete dev-cache targets (Xcode DerivedData, node_modules, Docker, simulators) and a live 'free scan / paid clean' that shows reclaimable GB before purchase.

Price at $29 one-time, single tier, 3-Mac license (band $25-39). No subscription. If recurring revenue is ever needed, use paid major-version upgrades, never a recurring license. This undercuts CleanMyMac's $39.95/yr and Sensei's $59 while staying clearly above the $9.99 toys.

Name shortlist to take to USPTO + domain checks, in priority order: Cairn (trust/safety angle), Vacuo (clean coinage), Derel/Derelict (developer wink at DerivedData), Husk, Vacate, Pareo, Spano. Treat Strato, Reclaim(r), and Sweepr as risky due to existing brands.
Hard-avoid list (confirmed same-category collisions): Cruft, Brisk, Scrub, Pry, MacSweep, Tidy Up, Mole — plus all named live competitors.

Differentiate on trust, not feature count: ship Apple-notarized, no telemetry, no account, no background daemon; make every deletion reviewable with exact paths and undoable. This is the explicit answer to why developers abandoned CleanMyMac and why they'd pay you over the free-but-abandoned OSS tools.

Before finalizing any name, run two checks I could not fully complete here: (1) USPTO TESS search in software classes 9/42, and (2) live domain availability for the .app/.dev/get<name>.com variants — several first-choice .coms are taken by unrelated firms.

bugs.title: AppleScript path injection in move_to_trash via unescaped f-string
bugs.detail: core/trash.py:29 interpolates the POSIX path directly into an AppleScript string literal: f'tell application "Finder" to delete (POSIX file "{posix}" as alias)'. Any path containing a double-quote breaks out of the literal. A file in ~/Downloads literally named 'evil" & (do shell script "...") & "x.dmg' produces a syntactically valid script that executes arbitrary AppleScript/shell as the user. Since filenames in Downloads are fully attacker-influenced (a malicious download), this is an arbitrary-code-execution path triggered by the user clicking 'Move to Trash'. Verified: the f-string yields '...POSIX file "/Users/me/Downloads/evil" & (do shell script "echo pwned") & "x.dmg" as alias'.
bugs.fix: Do not build AppleScript by string interpolation. Pass the path as an argument, not inside the script: subprocess.run(["osascript", "-e", 'on run argv', '-e', 'tell application "Finder" to delete (POSIX file (item 1 of argv) as alias)', '-e', 'end run', posix]). Better, drop osascript entirely and call the native Foundation API (Cocoa NSFileManager trashItemAtURL / Swift FileManager.trashItem in the native app), which both escapes nothing and preserves Put Back.

bugs.title: Orphaned-app-data heuristic produces false positives on live app data
bugs.detail: scanners/orphaned.py:62-77 flags any ~/Library/Application Support, Containers, and Group Containers folder whose name doesn't exactly match an installed CFBundleIdentifier. Verified failures with the owning apps INSTALLED: (1) human-named folders like 'Google' (Chrome's Application Support dir), 'Code', 'Steam' contain a dot test or no-dot suffix test that never matches a bundle id, so they are flagged 'No matching app installed'; (2) 'zoom.us' has a dot so it is compared by exact equality to bundle ids and fails (real id is us.zoom.xos); (3) Group Containers use team-id or group prefixes ('group.com.google.Chrome', 'ABCDE12345.com.google.Chrome') so exact match always fails. All flagged as orphans. They are Severity.REVIEW (not auto-selected), which limits accidental one-click deletion, but the label actively misinforms the user and invites bulk-select deletion of live app state (e.g. databases, license files).
bugs.fix: Match on bundle-id PREFIX, not equality: an installed id com.google.Chrome should claim folders named com.google.Chrome, com.google.Chrome.*, group.com.google.Chrome, and any <teamid>.com.google.Chrome. Strip leading team-id (10 alphanumerics) and 'group.' prefix before comparing, and treat a folder as claimed if any installed id startswith or contains the normalized name. Maintain an allowlist of human-named vendor folders ('Google','Mozilla','Microsoft','Steam', etc.) mapped to bundle prefixes. Only flag as orphan when confidence is high, and require last-modified age (e.g. untouched > 6 months) before suggesting.

bugs.title: Every directory is walked twice (size + mtime) — 2x scan time and IO
bugs.detail: dir_size() (core/fs.py:36) and latest_mtime() (core/fs.py:59) each do an independent full os.walk over the same tree. Every dir-yielding scanner calls both back-to-back per item: caches.py:48+50, dev_caches.py:54+56(latest_mtime arg), xcode.py:46+? (size then latest_mtime in the ScanItem ctor), browsers.py:42+? , orphaned.py:78+? , trash_scanner.py:30+? On large trees (Xcode DerivedData, npm cache, Maven .m2 with tens of thousands of files) this doubles wall-clock and disk IO. latest_mtime also re-stats every file a second time.
bugs.fix: Add a single function dir_stats(path) -> (total_size, latest_mtime) that walks once and accumulates both, using os.scandir() with DirEntry.stat() (one syscall per entry, caches results) instead of Path.stat(). Replace the dir_size()+latest_mtime() pairs in all six scanners with one dir_stats() call. In the native app use a single FileManager enumerator / fts(3) walk.

bugs.title: No Full Disk Access detection or guidance
bugs.detail: Scanners silently swallow PermissionError in dir_size (fs.py:54), latest_mtime (fs.py:76), and every iterdir/rglob (caches.py:37, orphaned.py:60, logs.py:27, etc.). On modern macOS, ~/Library/Caches, ~/Library/Containers, Safari data, and Mail/Messages are TCC-protected and unreadable without Full Disk Access. The app will report 0 B or partial sizes and the user has no idea the scan was crippled — it just looks like there's nothing to clean. This both undercounts recoverable space and can cause a delete to 'succeed' on a partial tree.
bugs.fix: Distinguish PermissionError (EACCES/EPERM) from other OSErrors and surface it. Probe a known-protected path (e.g. ~/Library/Containers/com.apple.Safari or ~/Library/Application Support/com.apple.TCC) at startup; if unreadable, show a banner with a deep link to System Settings > Privacy & Security > Full Disk Access (open 'x-apple.systempreferences:com.apple.preference.security?Privacy_AllFiles'). Track per-item 'incomplete (permission denied)' state so sizes aren't silently wrong.

bugs.title: safe_under_home allowlists system /Library/Caches for deletion
bugs.detail: core/fs.py:98-102 allowlists '/private/var/folders' and '/Library/Caches' (the root-level system cache, not the user's ~/Library/Caches). safe_under_home() is the sole guard used by both move_to_trash and permanent_delete (trash.py:20,61). Allowing the system-wide /Library/Caches means that if any scanner ever yields such a path (or a user adds one), permanent_delete would rmtree shared OS/daemon caches, which can destabilize the system and requires/encourages running with elevated privileges. No current scanner targets it, but the guard is meant to be the last line of defense and it is too permissive.
bugs.fix: Remove '/Library/Caches' from the allowlist (user caches live under HOME and are already covered). Keep the guard strictly to HOME plus the process-owned temp dir. Also resolve symlinks before the check (already done) AND verify the resolved real path still passes after resolution to defeat symlink-escape. Add an absolute denylist for ~/Library/{Mail,Messages,Photos,Application Support/MobileSync,Keychains} and ~/Library/Containers/com.apple.* in addition to the existing forbidden set.

bugs.title: Installer scanner marks generic .xz/.bz2 archives as SAFE and pre-selects them
bugs.detail: scanners/installers.py:12 includes bare '.xz' and '.bz2' in INSTALLER_SUFFIXES, and matched items are yielded with severity SAFE and selected=True (installers.py:52-54). Verified: 'myphotos.xz', 'important_notes.bz2', 'data.xz' all match. Any compressed data backup older than installers_age_days (default 30) in ~/Downloads is pre-checked for trashing. These are frequently user data archives, not installers. Combined with the trash flow this is a likely false-positive deletion of real data.
bugs.fix: Drop bare '.xz' and '.bz2' (and reconsider '.zip'/'.tar.gz', which are also common data archives). Restrict to disk-image/package installer types ('.dmg','.pkg','.iso'). For ambiguous archive types, downgrade to Severity.REVIEW and selected=False, and ideally confirm 'installer-likeness' (e.g. name matches a known app, or contains a .app/.pkg) before flagging.

bugs.title: Worker poll loop stops one cycle early, dropping the final DoneMessage handling path
bugs.detail: ui/app.py:210-220 _poll_worker drains the queue then schedules another poll only while self.worker.is_running(). The worker thread sets DoneMessage and then the thread exits; there is a race where is_running() becomes False before the last queued messages (final ItemMessage/CategoryDoneMessage/DoneMessage) are drained, so the next after() is never scheduled and those messages sit in the queue unprocessed — progressbar may never stop and buttons stay disabled. The broad 'except Exception: pass' at app.py:217 also hides queue/Tk errors.
bugs.fix: After the worker is no longer running, drain the queue one final time before stopping the poll loop; or key the loop off having seen a DoneMessage rather than thread liveness. Catch only queue.Empty in the drain loop, not bare Exception.

bugs.title: Deletion summary counts/sizes are computed via path.exists() races and lose per-category accounting
bugs.detail: ui/app.py:429-454 _perform: (a) sets item.size = 0 to 'mark gone' then immediately rebuilds the category by filtering on item.path.exists() (app.py:448) — for move_to_trash the file is gone so it is dropped, but the sidebar total is recomputed from total_size which now reads the still-listed-but-zeroed items inconsistently; (b) it only ever operates on the CURRENT category's selected items (_selected_items reads self.current_category, app.py:378-382), so a user who selected items across multiple categories in the sidebar loses the other categories' selections on delete — only the visible category is acted on, silently. There is no cross-category 'Clean All'.
bugs.fix: Operate over all categories' selected items, not just the current one (iterate self.categories.values()). Track success by catching the action's exceptions rather than re-probing exists() (which races and misreports network/permission cases). Recompute totals from the surviving item list after removal.

bugs.title: Docker sentinel item is RISKY but still counts toward 'Recoverable' total incorrectly handled / dead selection logic
bugs.detail: dev_caches.py:84-93 yields a synthetic Docker info item with size=0, severity RISKY, path pointing at a non-existent sentinel ~/Library/Caches/.macsweep_docker_info. It cannot be selected (toggle blocks RISKY, app.py:313) and size 0 means it adds nothing to totals — fine — but it clutters the list, and if a user ever Reveals it, 'open -R' fails silently. More importantly it conflates 'information' with 'scan items' in the same model with no dedicated info/advice type.
bugs.fix: Introduce a distinct 'advice'/'info' item kind (or an is_actionable flag on ScanItem) instead of overloading a fake path + RISKY severity. Render advice rows separately so they aren't mistaken for deletable items.

bugs.title: latest_mtime/dir_size symlink handling and is_file() follow symlinks
bugs.detail: core/fs.py:65 latest_mtime uses path.is_file() which follows symlinks; if the scanned root is itself a symlink to a file it returns that target's mtime, and for a symlinked dir it will os.walk the target (followlinks defaults False so it won't descend, but the top-level stat at line 61 follows the link). dir_size skips symlinked files (fs.py:49) but os.walk(followlinks=False) still lists symlinked subdirs' names without descending — acceptable, but size of a symlinked dir target is silently 0, which can under-report. Minor correctness/under-counting.
bugs.fix: Use os.lstat / Path.is_symlink() checks consistently at the root, and decide deliberately whether to resolve and size symlink targets (and guard against symlink loops with a visited-inode set).

reusableIP.category: Developer-cache target list (npm/pip/cargo/gradle/etc.) with per-target severity and remediation notes
reusableIP.notes: High-value curated knowledge: 17 package-manager/build-tool cache locations with relative paths, a SAFE/REVIEW classification, and a human note that often names the proper CLI cleanup command (e.g. 'pnpm store prune', 'brew cleanup', 'docker system prune'). Port this table verbatim into the native app's data model. Note pnpm/Gradle/Maven/Deno are correctly marked REVIEW because they are content-addressed stores or local repos, not pure throwaway caches — that nuance is the valuable part. Also worth porting: the Docker 'system df' read-only advice pattern (report reclaimable space, never auto-delete).

reusableIP.category: Xcode/CoreSimulator junk targets with severity rationale
reusableIP.notes: 7 Xcode targets (DerivedData SAFE; iOS/watchOS/tvOS DeviceSupport, Archives, CoreSimulator Devices REVIEW) with concise rationale for each ('Build outputs Xcode rebuilds on demand', 'keep recent archives if you ship apps'). The whole-scanner short-circuit when ~/Library/Developer doesn't exist (skip if Xcode not installed) is good product behavior to keep. DerivedData being the one auto-selected SAFE target reflects real-world safety.

reusableIP.category: Three-tier severity model (SAFE / REVIEW / RISKY) driving default selection and delete-ability
reusableIP.notes: Clean, portable safety taxonomy: Severity enum gates UI behavior — SAFE may be pre-selected, REVIEW shown unchecked, RISKY never selectable/deletable (enforced in UI toggle and select-all). This 'review-first, never auto-delete risky' philosophy is the product's core trust mechanism and should anchor the native app. Selected-by-default policy lives per-scanner (xcode SAFE auto-selects, installers/logs/trash auto-select) which is a reasonable default-aggressiveness dial.

Single chokepoint guard used by BOTH move_to_trash and permanent_delete: resolves the path, requires it under HOME (or a small allowlist), blocks HOME itself, and denylists ~/Library/Keychains, ~/.ssh, ~/Documents. The pattern (one authoritative guard all destructive ops must pass) is excellent and should be ported — but harden it per the bugs (drop system /Library/Caches from allowlist, expand denylist to Mail/Messages/Photos/MobileSync/Containers/com.apple.*, re-check after symlink resolution).

reusableIP.category: Orphaned-app-data heuristic (bundle-id reconciliation against installed apps)
reusableIP.notes: The CONCEPT is valuable: enumerate installed apps' CFBundleIdentifier from /Applications + ~/Applications Info.plist, then reconcile against ~/Library/{Application Support,Containers,Group Containers} to find leftover data for uninstalled apps. The exclusion of com.apple.* and known system folders (MobileSync, CrashReporter, iCloud) is good. The matching logic itself is buggy (see bugs) — port the data sources and the com.apple exclusion, but rewrite the matcher to use bundle-id prefix matching, strip team-id/'group.' prefixes, map human-named vendor folders, and require staleness before flagging.

reusableIP.category: Trash strategy: Finder 'Put Back'-preserving delete with manual fallback + typed-confirm for large permanent deletes
reusableIP.notes: Two-tier delete strategy worth porting: prefer Finder-mediated trash (preserves the OS 'Put Back' restore metadata) and fall back to a manual move into ~/.Trash with timestamp de-duplication of name collisions (trash.py:_manual_trash). empty_trash() returns reclaimed bytes. UI requires typing 'DELETE' for permanent deletes over 1 GB (app.py:_ask_typed_confirm) — a good friction-for-destructive-action pattern. In the native app, replace osascript with FileManager.trashItem (gets Put Back for free and removes the injection risk) but keep the size-up-to-permanent fallback, name-collision handling, and reclaimed-bytes accounting.

reusableIP.category: Browser-cache target list and cache-vs-state separation
reusableIP.notes: Curated per-browser cache paths (Safari/Chrome/Firefox/Brave/Arc/Edge/Opera) including the tricky Chrome subpaths (Code Cache, GPUCache, Service Worker CacheStorage under Application Support, not just Library/Caches). Crucially, browsers are EXCLUDED from the generic App Caches scanner (caches.py EXCLUDE set) so they're handled by the dedicated, careful list — that 'route browsers to a specialist scanner' decision avoids nuking cookies/profile state and is worth keeping.

reusableIP.category: Pluggable scanner architecture (registry + base class + streaming worker)
reusableIP.notes: Clean extensibility pattern: @register decorator collects scanner factories, discover() imports modules to self-register, each Scanner yields ScanItems lazily, and a background worker streams ProgressMessage/ItemMessage/CategoryStart/Done over a queue to a polling UI thread (cancellable via threading.Event). Settings singleton with type-coerced getters and per-category size/age thresholds + excluded_paths. The model (streaming results, cancel token, per-scanner thresholds) maps directly onto a Swift async-sequence / actor design.

gaps: No tests whatsoever — the tests/ directory is empty. Safety-critical delete/guard logic (safe_under_home, trash escaping, orphaned matcher) has zero coverage. A cleaner that deletes files MUST have a tested safety harness.

No undo / restore tracking beyond relying on macOS Trash. Permanent delete is irreversible with only a typed-confirm gate. Competitive cleaners keep a removal log / quarantine so users can review and roll back what was cleaned.

No size accuracy via APFS awareness — uses logical st_size, ignores APFS clones/sparse files/compression and hardlinks (files counted multiple times). Reported 'recoverable' space will overstate actual freed space; competitors measure on-disk (allocated) size and dedup hardlinks.

No Full Disk Access onboarding/permission flow (see bug) — a native cleaner needs a first-run TCC prompt + Privacy settings deep-link, otherwise it silently sees almost nothing on a default macOS install.

No application uninstaller — finding orphaned data is only half the job; users expect 'drag app here / select app -> remove app + all its caches, prefs, containers, login items, launch agents'. There is no app-centric uninstall flow, only leftover-detection.

Missing high-value scan categories competitors ship: duplicate-file finder, large-folder/disk treemap visualization, mail/iMessage attachment cleanup, iOS device backups (~/Library/Application Support/MobileSync/Backup), language-file (.lproj) stripping, broken login items / launch agents, leftover kernel extensions, and Time Machine local snapshots (tmutil).
No scheduling / background monitoring / menu-bar agent — competitive utilities offer periodic scans, low-disk alerts, and a menu-bar quick-clean. This is a one-shot foreground Tk app.

No real packaging, signing, notarization, or sandbox/entitlements story — pyproject builds a console script only; there is no .app bundle, code signing, notarization, hardened runtime, or App Sandbox temporary-exception design. Required for distribution and for the FDA permission to even work.
No localization, accessibility (VoiceOver), or Retina/dark-mode-aware UI — the Tk 'aqua' theme with hardcoded hex colors won't adapt to macOS appearance; a native SwiftUI/AppKit rewrite is implied.

No safety net for files currently in use / open by other processes, no detection of iCloud-dataless (evicted) files (deleting a dataless placeholder can purge cloud-only data semantics), and no check for files inside .app bundles being referenced — large_files.py only skips paths containing '.app' by string match, which is brittle.

No per-item provenance / 'why is this safe to delete' explanation surfaced richly in UI beyond a one-line note, and no aggregated 'clean all categories' action — deletion is scoped to the currently viewed category only (see bug), so there's no single trusted one-click clean.

SAFETY HOLE — `safeToTrash` HOME-confinement breaks legitimate dev targets. The spec's chokepoint guard 're-verify the resolved real path is under HOME and not in the denylist.' But several v1 targets are NOT under HOME: simulator runtimes live under `/Library/Developer/CoreSimulator` (spec even says SIP-protected), the Docker.raw advice card, system caches mentioned for v2, and per-project trees on external/secondary APFS volumes (`/Volumes/...`). A dev with repos on an external SSD (very common on 256/512 GB Macs — the exact target buyer) will have node_modules/target/ that the guard silently refuses to trash. The guard as written either blocks real targets or has to carve out exceptions that reintroduce the risk it exists to prevent. Needs an explicit per-scanner allowlist-of-roots model, not a single HOME check.

SAFETY HOLE — Trash on a different volume than the file is not free and can fail. `FileManager.trashItem` moving a file from an external/secondary APFS volume goes to that volume's `/Volumes/X/.Trashes/<uid>`, not `~/.Trash`. For a cross-volume move it is a copy+delete (slow, needs 2x transient space), and APFS clones/hardlinks are NOT preserved across volumes — so 'trash-not-delete' can momentarily DOUBLE disk usage on the volume you're trying to free, or fail with ENOSPC on a nearly-full disk (the literal scenario the app targets). The spec never addresses cross-volume trash, low-space trash failure, or that the 'reclaim' only lands after Empty Trash which itself needs the space to exist. This is a headline-promise failure: 'Reclaim 84 GB' then trashItem fails at 98% full.

SAFETY HOLE — node_modules 'SAFE iff sibling lockfile present' is wrong for monorepos and pnpm workspaces. In pnpm/yarn-workspace/npm-workspace monorepos the lockfile lives ONLY at the repo root, while `packages/*/node_modules` have no sibling lockfile. The spec's rule would mark every workspace package's node_modules as REVIEW (false alarm) OR, worse, the inverse heuristic could mark a vendored runtime as SAFE. Also misses: `node_modules/.bin` symlinks, `node_modules` containing patch-package patches or locally-linked (`npm link`) packages that do NOT regenerate from install. 'Regenerates' is materially false for `npm link`, `file:` deps, and patched packages.

SAFETY HOLE — Xcode DerivedData is labeled the #1 SAFE quick win, but DerivedData can hold the only copy of uncommitted state in some workflows (SwiftPM resolved-package state, `.swiftpm` user data, and crucially XCTest result bundles / coverage from CI-less local runs). More concretely, blanket-trashing DerivedData while Xcode is OPEN corrupts the live build and can crash Xcode mid-index. The spec never says 'require Xcode/Simulator/the relevant app be quit' as a hard gate for DerivedData, IDE caches, or CoreSimulator — it says it only for simctl/Simulator. Cleaning a live app's cache directory is a known corruption vector.

MISSING SAFETY GATE — no handling of in-use / locked files and partial-delete atomicity. Deleting a directory tree while a process holds files open (Docker daemon, a running dev server, a build) yields partially-deleted trees that DON'T regenerate cleanly and may leave the toolchain in a broken state requiring manual `rm -rf` + reinstall. The spec has no 'is this tool currently running?' check, no per-tree transactional semantics, and no recovery story for a half-trashed `~/.cargo` or `~/go/pkg/mod` (which is mode-0444 — trashItem may fail mid-tree leaving it half-gone).

DIFFERENTIATION GAP — the 'maintained safety database keyed by macOS version + bundle id' is asserted but has no maintenance mechanism, and the app ships with NO telemetry/account. A curated path database for dozens of toolchains rots fast (paths move every Xcode/Node/Docker release). With no telemetry, no crash reporting, and no auto-update in v1 (Sparkle is explicitly v2), a solo dev cannot detect when a path moved or a delete started failing in the field. The single biggest claimed moat over free OSS — 'maintained, tested safety database' — has no operational plan and no update channel in v1. This is the differentiation's load-bearing wall and it's hollow.

MONETIZATION RISK — free-scan/paid-clean is trivially defeated and the audience knows it. The wedge buyer is a developer who, once shown 'DerivedData 35 GB, node_modules 9 GB' with exact paths in the free scan, can `rm -rf` those exact paths in 10 seconds for $0. The free tier hands the power-user the entire actionable output (paths + sizes + the correct CLI method, which the spec prints in every table) and asks them to pay $29 to run `trash` instead of `rm`. The very transparency that builds trust destroys the conversion lever for this specific audience. Pearcleaner/npkill being free and 'validating demand' cuts the other way — it proves this audience expects free.

PRICING/REVENUE RISK — $29 one-time with no recurring revenue, no telemetry, no account, against a category that demands continuous maintenance. GTM.md's own honest number is 100-400 units in 14 days. At $29 minus Polar MoR fees that is roughly $2.6k-$10k, one-time, to fund perpetual maintenance of a path database across an OS and a dozen ecosystems that change quarterly. The 'paid major-version upgrade' escape hatch (Sketch/Sublime model) is hand-waved to v2 and historically underperforms for utilities. The economics of 'maintained forever, one-time $29, no telemetry to even know it broke' do not close.

INFEASIBILITY — the FDA detection probe is partly wrong. The spec proposes test-reading `~/Library/Safari/Bookmarks.plist` AND `/Library/Preferences/com.apple.TimeMachine.plist` as FDA probes. Verified on this machine: `/Library/Preferences/com.apple.TimeMachine.plist` is `root:wheel 0644` and world-readable, so reading it succeeds WITHOUT Full Disk Access — it's a false-positive probe that will report FDA granted when it isn't. `~/Library/Safari/` is the correct TCC-gated probe; the TimeMachine path should be dropped. Also: `~/Library/Caches` itself is NOT FDA-gated (it's user-owned 0700) — many dev caches under `~/.npm`, `~/.cargo`, `~/go` are plain user dirs needing no FDA at all, so the 'everything needs FDA' framing overstates the permission wall and may push an unnecessary scary prompt.

INFEASIBILITY/UNDER-SPEC — shelling out to `docker`, `brew`, `pnpm`, `go`, `simctl`, `xcrun` from a notarized non-sandboxed GUI app is fragile and under-specified. Issues the spec ignores: (1) these tools may be installed via asdf/mise/Homebrew/Volta with shims that only resolve under the user's interactive shell init — an absolute `/opt/homebrew/bin/pnpm` may not exist (pnpm via corepack, node via nvm, etc.); the spec's 'absolute executableURL' assumption fails for shimmed toolchains. (2) `xcrun simctl`/`runtime delete` can hang or prompt; no timeout/cancellation contract is specified beyond the prototype's 8s. (3) Running `docker system prune -a --volumes` from a GUI tool is itself a data-loss vector (named volumes = local DB data) — offering it behind a checkbox is exactly the 'reckless cleaner' behavior the brand promises to avoid.

MISSING CLEANING CATEGORIES (developer) — notable omissions a power-user will immediately list: Android SDK/AVD system images + emulator (`~/Library/Android/sdk`, `~/.android/avd` — 10-40 GB, huge for RN/Flutter/mobile devs), Flutter/Dart pub cache (`~/.pub-cache`, `~/.gradle` Flutter artifacts), Xcode beta/multiple-version installs and old Command Line Tools, `~/Library/Developer/CoreSimulator/Caches/dyld` specifically, Carthage (`~/Library/Caches/org.carthage.CarthageKit`), `.swiftpm` and SPM artifact cache vs the one listed, Bazel (`~/.cache/bazel`, can be 50+ GB), ccache, Nix store (`/nix` — explicitly NOT user-deletable, a trap), Composer (`~/.composer/cache`), NuGet (`~/.nuget`), `.dotnet`, Sourcetree/Tower repo caches, Postman/Insomnia, TablePlus, and Electron app caches (Slack/Discord/Notion/VS Code each cache GBs). The 'developer-native depth' wedge has visible holes.

MISSING CLEANING CATEGORIES (general/Apple) — the biggest real-world space hogs on the target 256/512 GB Macs are barely addressed: (1) `~/Library/Group Containers/...group.com.apple.notes`, Photos library bloat, and especially **Mail downloads / attachments** (deferred to v2) — often 20-80 GB. (2) Time Machine local snapshots are listed as read-only 'managed by macOS', but on a capacity-constrained Mac thinning local snapshots (`tmutil thinlocalsnapshots`) is frequently THE single biggest reclaim and the #1 cause of the 'System Data' the positioning explicitly promises to explain — surfacing it read-only under-delivers on the stated wedge. (3) iCloud Drive 'Optimize Storage' evicted-then-redownloaded files and `~/Library/Caches/CloudKit`. (4) Sleepimage/swap, old iOS .ipsw firmware in `~/Library/iTunes`.
risks: DATA-LOSS, HIGH: The cross-volume trash + low-disk-space failure mode (trashItem copy+delete needs transient 2x space; clones not preserved across volumes; ENOSPC on a near-full disk) can lose data or strand a half-moved tree precisely when the user is most desperate. The 'always Trash, recoverable' safety promise quietly does not hold across volumes or near capacity — and 'near capacity' is the product's entire reason to exist.

DATA-LOSS, HIGH: `safeToTrash`'s single HOME-confinement rule is in direct conflict with v1 targets that live outside HOME (simulator runtimes under /Library, repos on /Volumes external SSDs, Docker.raw). Whatever carve-out makes those work reintroduces exactly the over-permissive guard called out as prototype BUG-002. There is no specified reconciliation; this is the most likely place a real deletion of real data slips through.

DATA-LOSS, MEDIUM: Cleaning DerivedData / CoreSimulator / IDE caches while the owning app (Xcode, Simulator, VS Code) is RUNNING corrupts live state. Spec gates only simctl on 'quit Simulator first' and never generalizes the running-process check. A locked/open file mid-tree-trash leaves a partially-deleted toolchain that does not regenerate.

REGENERATION-CLAIM RISK, MEDIUM: Multiple SAFE items do NOT actually regenerate cleanly — `npm link`/`file:`/patch-package node_modules, monorepo workspace packages (lockfile-at-root heuristic misfires), and `.venv`/conda envs that are the only copy of a resolved environment. Mislabeling these SAFE/pre-checked breaks builds and erodes the trust that is the brand's only moat. One viral 'Cairn nuked my monorepo' post ends the product.

TRUST/LEGAL RISK, MEDIUM: Offering `docker system prune -a --volumes` (destroys named volumes = local DB data) and any blanket DerivedData/cache sweep means a single mislabeled-SAFE incident produces real, irreversible loss for a vocal, technical audience that will publish it. For a solo studio whose entire positioning is 'the safe one,' this is existential reputational risk with no telemetry to even detect it happening in the field.

MONETIZATION RISK, HIGH: Free-scan-shows-exact-paths-and-CLI / paid-clean is self-defeating for power users who can `rm -rf` the revealed paths for free; combined with $29-one-time / no-telemetry / no-recurring-revenue against a category needing perpetual quarterly maintenance, the unit economics (100-400 units per GTM.md) do not fund the maintenance the differentiation depends on.

INFEASIBILITY RISK, MEDIUM: Verified false-positive in the FDA probe (`/Library/Preferences/com.apple.TimeMachine.plist` is world-readable, so it reports FDA-granted when it isn't); plus brittle absolute-path assumptions for shimmed toolchains (corepack/nvm/asdf/mise/Volta) mean docker/pnpm/node/brew invocations will fail or no-op on a large fraction of real dev setups, silently undercounting or erroring the headline reclaim figure.

DIFFERENTIATION RISK, MEDIUM: The 'maintained, tested safety database' moat over free OSS has no maintenance/update mechanism in v1 (no telemetry, no crash reporting, Sparkle auto-update deferred to v2). A path database that cannot be observed or updated in the field rots into the same 'abandonment-prone' state the spec criticizes Pearcleaner/DevCleaner for.

SCOPE/COMPETITIVE RISK, LOW-MEDIUM: Visible category gaps (Android SDK/AVD, Bazel, Nix-as-a-trap, pub-cache, Mail attachments, TM local-snapshot thinning) undercut both the 'developer-native depth' claim and the 'explain System Data' general-user promise; reviewers comparing against CleanMyMac/OmniDiskSweeper will list these immediately.

NAMING/IP RISK, LOW-MEDIUM: 'Cairn' is self-flagged MEDIUM TM risk and the spec hasn't run the USPTO class-9/42 + domain checks it prescribes; shipping the brand before clearing it risks a forced rename after launch SEO/Product Hunt equity is built.
missingFeatures: Cross-volume and low-disk-space trash strategy: detect target volume, fall back behavior when trash would exceed free space, and an honest 'this needs N GB free to safely trash' precondition before promising reclaim.
A 'tool is currently running' / open-file guard before cleaning any app-owned cache (Xcode, Simulator, Docker daemon, VS Code, JetBrains, running dev servers), with a quit-first prompt.

An update + integrity channel for the safety path database (even without telemetry): a signed remote JSON the app fetches so moved/renamed paths and new toolchains can ship without a full app update; plus opt-in crash/error reporting so field failures are detectable.

Monorepo/workspace-aware regeneration model for node_modules/.venv (root-lockfile detection, pnpm workspace globs, npm/yarn workspaces) instead of a sibling-lockfile-only heuristic; detection of npm link / file: / patch-package as non-regenerable.
Missing dev categories: Android SDK + AVD images, Flutter/pub-cache, Bazel, ccache, Carthage, Composer, NuGet/.dotnet, Electron-app caches, multiple-Xcode + old Command Line Tools, .ipsw firmware.

Time Machine local-snapshot thinning as an actionable (not read-only) reclaim with explicit consequences — it's frequently the single largest reclaim on capacity-constrained Macs and central to the promised 'System Data' explainer.

Correct, verified FDA detection probe set (drop the world-readable TimeMachine plist; use only genuinely TCC-gated paths) plus per-scanner declaration of which categories actually need FDA vs. plain user dirs.
